Vs.
Chowdhury Tanbir Ahmed Siddiky ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 30th June 1988 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 896 of 1973)
full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Choudhury, J:- This appeal by leave, has been filed by Bangladesh against the judgment and order dated 30 June 1988 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 896 of 1973 setting aside in part the order of abatement of Title Suit No. 81 of 1968 made by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka on 21 April 1973.

2. The subject matter consists of rent receiving interest in different touzis taluks and tenures in different shares and also khas lands of different kinds comprising two wakf estates, one wakf lillah created by the great grand father of the plaintiff and the other wakf alal-aulad by his grand father. The plaintiff who is the respondent happens to be the mutawalli of the said two estates known as Baliade Wakf estates. He brought the suit against the Province of East Pakistan and the Deputy commissioner, Dhaka praying for the following reliefs:

(i) a declaration that no valid compensation Assessment Roll in respect of the Properties in suit has been prepared and finally published within the meaning of Section 43 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, and the plaintiff's right to possess and manage the said properties has not been affected by the publication of the compensation assessment Roll as claimed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2;

(ii) a further declaration that the plaintiff has the right to continue with the maintenance and management of the religious institution of wakf in respect of the properties described in the schedule and that the defendants have no right to interfere with the plaintiff's said right of maintenance and management of the wakfs;

(iii) an order of perpetual injunction restraining defendant Nos. 1 and 2 from interfering in any manner with the plaintiff's possession in the wakf properties described in schedule Nos. I and II in the plaint.

3. The background of the case is this: On 2 April 1956 the then Government of East Pakistan issued two notifications in respect of each district of the Province, one under sub-section (1) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, briefly the Act, acquiring the rent receiving interests of all rent receivers and the other under sub-section (2) of the said section acquiring all khas lands of these rent receivers, except those retainable by them under sub-section (2), clauses (a) and (b) of section 20 the Act, both effective from 14 April 1956. The plaintiff challenged the notifications so far as those related to his wakf estates in Writ Petition No. 80 of 1957, but following the decision of the Supreme Court in the Province of East Pakistan Vs. Mohammad Mehadi Ali Khan Panni, (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 318 it had abated after the abrogation of the constitution of 1956.

4. On 24 May 1960 Ordinance IX of 1960 was promulgated, amending the Act by adding a new section 10A and on 7 February 1962 on further amendment of the said provision by Ordinance IV of 1962 it was provided that where the rent receiving interests held under any wakf, debutter or other religious trusts, had been acquired under sub-section (I) of section 3 of the Act, but the provincial Government had not exercised the right of possession over such interest the mutawallis, shebaits or trustees, as the case may be, holding such interests on the date of acquisition, shall continue and be deemed to have continued to manage such interest, as agents of the provincial Government, till the last day of the agricultural year, next following the date of the publication of the notification under sub-section (2) section 43 of chapter V of the Act.

5. Meanwhile preparation of records of rights under Chapter IV and thereafter, of compensation assessment rolls under Chapter V was undertaken by the Government, and this culminated in the issue of notifications under Sub-Section (2) of Section 43 of the Ac, declaring that the compensation assessment rolls had been finally published. All the notification were published in the Official Gazette by the year 1963 purportedly vesting in the Government all non retainable interests in the estates of all districts other than those already acquired under chapter II with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the official Gazette.

6. The Government of East Pakistan thereafter tried to take over possession of the disputed properties with effect from 14 April 1964. The plaintiff challenged the action in Writ Petition No. 146 of 1964. After having failed to obtain any relief therein he preferred Civil Appeal No. 27-D of 1965. After an analogous hearing of this appeal along with other similar matters the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 26 February 1968 holding that the vesting of the properties in question in the Government either under notifications issued under chapter II, or under Chapter V, on the relevant dates, was complete and final. The decision was reported as Chowdhury Tanbir Ahmed Siddiky Vs. The Province of East Pakistan, (1968) 20 DLR (SC) at page 144. In the consolidated judgment, in reply to an argument made from the side of one of the parties that proper compensation assessment rolls had not been prepared in the case, the court observed at page 163 as follows:

This is a vague and infinity ground, and no attempt was made at any stage of these case to make out precisely the reasons for holding that the publication of compensation assessment rolls was open to any legal exception. If however, there be any such defeat in the proceedings which culminated in the publication of those rolls it would still be open to the appellants to agitate the matter in the proper forum" (see para 34 of the report).

7. In this context the plaintiff brought the suit with the aforementioned prayers contending that the preparation of the compensation assessment rolls in respect of the wakf estates in question and their publication were not done in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules framed there under and that the plaintiff had continued to possess the properties, even after the aforesaid notifications, undisturbed and unhampered, by realizing rents and tolls etc. It was also contend that the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B. Ord. No. 111 of 1956) whereby section 3 of the Act was amended was itself an invalid piece of legislation and therefore the notifications of acquisition under the amended section were it invalid.

8. The claims of the plaintiff were denied by the defendants in a written statement.

9. The suit remained pending till after the liberation of the country. On 16 June 1972 the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (second) Order, 1972 briefly President's Order No. 69 of 1972 was promulgated. Read with the amendment thereof by president's Order No. 97 of 1972 Article 4 of the said Order reads as under:

"(1) subject to clause (2) any legal proceedings which are pending by or against the erstwhile Government or Pakistan or the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan in any court of Tribunal or before any arbitrator, tax authority or other authority, in Bangladesh shall be continued by or against the Government of Bangladesh and the Government of Bangladesh shall be deemed to be substituted for the government of Pakistan or, as the case may be, the Government of East Pakistan as a party to such proceedings.

(2) The Government of Bangladesh may, at any time before the final hearing of any legal proceedings mentioned in clause (1) submit a written application to the court, Tribunal, arbitrator, tax authority or other authority in or before which such legal proceedings are pending stating that the Government of Bangladesh shall not be a party to the proceedings and with effect from the date of submission of such application the Government of Bangladesh shall cease to be a party to such proceedings and, if such proceedings cannot continue in the absence of the Government of Bangladesh, the proceeding shall abate."

10. On 3 August, 1972 the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order, 1972 briefly President's Order No. 90 of 1972 came into force. Article 2 of this order provides as follows:

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceeding pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (E. B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951) or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B Ord. No. 111 of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders, passed in such suits, appeals applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect and no court shall entertain, and no person shall bring any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question.

11. In the light of these statutory provisions and against the factual background outlined above the Government of Bangladesh made two applications, one under Article 4(2) of President's order No. 69 of 1972 on 30 August 1972 and another under Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 on 30 September 1972 seeking abatement of the suit.

12. Both the applications came up for hearing on 21 April 1973 when the learned Subordinate Judge recorded an order of abatement of the whole suit.

13. Against the said order the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No. 896 of 1973. By the impugned judgment and order a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute in part and set aside the order of abatement in so far as recording abatement of the whole suit, it was further ordered that paragraphs 14-16 and prayer No. (ii) of the plaint would stand abated under article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972, but that the rest of the suit would survive. The learned Judge took the view that "the Government's application under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 was not maintainable because in any view of the matter the later law (President's Order No. 90 of 1972) has abrogated the earlier law (President's Order No. 69 of 1972) in so far as suits of the category "mentioned in Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 are concerned, because the provisions of the two Acts with regard to such suits are mutually inconsistent". The learned Judge was also of the view that the averments in paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint and prayer No. (ii) thereof could not survive as the plaintiff had clearly challenged the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) ordinance, 1956 (E.B. ordinance no. III of 1956)" in a speculative manner, devised as an after thought, formulated upon a chance information."

14. Appearing on behalf of the appellant Mr. A.W. Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney General, submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division was not correct in his views respecting the application of the Government under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 and the reasoning therefore given by him. He further submits that the learned judge erred in not following the decision in the People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Sri Modan Gopal Jew Bigraha and others, 33 DLR (AD) 13 and holding that in view of the plaintiff's main prayer, claiming immunity from acquisition, along with other ancillary or consequential prayers the suit stood abated as a whole under Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972.

15. In reply Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned counsel for the respondent, contends that in the suit there were facts alleged and prayers made which could be gone into by the court without deciding the question of acquisition in question and those reliefs could be granted even without questioning the acquisition of the wakf estates. The learned counsel however had not much to argue against the abatement of the suit under Article 4(2) of President's Order 69 of 1972.

16. The moot question that arises there fore is whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division was justified in not affirming the order of abatement of the whole suit passed by the trial court under article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 and Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972.

<u>17. From a mere reading of the provisions of the two President's Orders quoted earlier it is clear that President's Order No. 69 of 1972 envisages abatement of all kinds of suits or other legal proceedings against the Government of Bangladesh whether or not related to acquisition under the Act when the Government opts not to be a party thereto, while President's Order No. 90 of 1972 seeks abatement only of suits and other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of the legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (E. b. Act No. XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E. b. Ord. No III of 1956) or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question President's Order No. 69 of 1972 covers a much bigger filed than president Order No. 90 of 1972. President's Order No. 90 of 1972 is a specie. Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 begins with the phrase "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". Such a non obstinate clause, it is true, has the effect of abrogating the provisions of a prior statue in the event of a conflict between the same and the new statue. But such a non obstinate clause cannot reasonable be read as overriding anything contained in any relevant existing law which is not inconsistent with the new statute. We are unable to see any inconsistency or mutual exclusiveness between the two President's Orders both of which aim at abatement of a suit. As a logical sequel the provisions of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 cannot be said to have been abrogated because of the non obstinate clause added to President Order No. 90 of 1972.</u>

<u>18. The instant suit was instituted against the Province of East Pakistan and the Deputy commissioner of Dhaka By virtue of clause (1) of Article 4 of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 Bangladesh was deemed to be substituted for the province of East Pakistan, but clause (2) left an option to the government of Bangladesh not to be impleaded in which case the suit was to abate as a whole if it was not maintainable against the rest of the defendants. In this case bereft of the Government of Bangladesh there are no parties against whom suit could continue. The Government having submitted as written application to the court stating that it would not be a party to the proceeding the suit as a whole abated with effect from the date of submission of such application.</u>

19. One might notice that although redundant, the Government of Bangladesh made an application for abatement of the suit even under President's Order No. 90 of 1972. Therefore, we have to look into the facts disclosed in the plaint and the prayers made therein to whether the plaint was hit by the President's Order No. 90 of 1972. The learned Judge of the High Court Division opined that paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint and prayer No. (ii) thereof came within the mischief of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 and not the rest of the allegations and the prayers. We think that not only the allegations in paragraphs 14-16 and prayer No. (ii) had abated but also the suit itself had abated as a whole, being hit by Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972. The averments in the plaint and the prayers made therein amount to a challenge of the acquisition of the wakf estates concerned, apart from a challenge of E.B. Ordinance No. III of 1956 as noticed by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. In the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs. Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigrahah and others. 33 DLR (AD) 13 this court had the occasion to consider the question of abatement of a suit under President's Order No. 90 of 1972 in a similar case. The prayers in that case were couched in more or less identical terms as in the present case. The plaint of that suit was found to have been hit by president's Order No. 90 of 1972.

20. The plaintiff has also not set up any case claiming benefit of section 10A of the Act or having applied to the Collector expressing his intention to avail himself of the entitlement to any benefit there under, as required under subsection (11) thereof.

<u>21. Incidentally it may be observed once notification under sub-section (2) of section 43 of the Act is published in the official Gazette, such notification is conclusive proof of such publication and of the date thereof and section 72 of the Act bars a Civil Court from entertaining any suit "in respect of the preparation signing and publication of a Compensation Assessment roll or any part thereof under Chapter V or Chapter VA or in respect of any entry in or omission from such roll."</u>

<u>22. Again, partial abatement of a suit does not seem to have been contemplated under President's Order No. 90 of 1972.</u>

For the above reasons the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and order of the High Court Division be set aside and the order of the trial court be restored.

End.

lawyer:
Abdus Salam Mondal, Deputy Attorney General instructed by Ms. Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the petitioner Nurul Islam,

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 04.07.2010 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in A.A.T. Appeal No. 14 of 2007)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 04.07.2010 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in A.A.T. Appeal No. 14 of 2007 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and order dated 30.10.2006 passed by the Administrative Tribunal No.  2, Dhaka in Administrative Tribunal Case No. 112 of 2005.

2. The relevant facts in brief are as follows:

<u>3. One Md. Sadekur Rahman, Inspector, Customs and Excise and VAT Commissioner ate, Sylhet as petitioner filed a case being Administrative Tribunal Case No. 28 of 2003 which was renumbered as Administrative Tribunal Case No. 112 of 2005 upon claiming that the persons serving in the National Board of Revenue (NBR) being Class I and Class II gazette officers were not classified within a combined gradation list and promotion from Class II post to Class I post was being done at the whims and caprice of the authority. He, therefore, claimed that there should be a combined gradation list in accordance with the Non-cadre Class I and II Gazetted Officers (Customs Excise and VAT) Appointment and Service Terms and Conditions Act of 2000 (Act No. XX of 2000) The Administrative Tribunal upon hearing both the parties allowed the application in part and directed that all Class II non-cadre officers under the NBR should be listed in a combined gradation list. The NBR did not challenge the decision of the Administrative Tribunal. However, one Lucky Chakma, respondent No. 1 herein, who was not a party before the Administrative Tribunal, preferred appeal against the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal. By the impugned order passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in A.A.T. Appeal. No. 14 of 2007, the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal was set aside on the ground of defect of parties.</u>

4. Mr. Abdus Salam Mondal, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing before us on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the Administrative Tribunal allowed the case of Md. Sadekur Rahman in part directing the authority to formulate a combined gradation list in respect of Class II non-cadre officers i.e. Appraiser, Inspector, Preventive and Intelligence Officer, and the authority concerned did not prefer any appeal. On the other hand, the respondent No. 1, who was not a party before the Administrative Tribunal, instead of filing any case before the Administrative Tribunal to air her grievance, preferred Appeal No. 14 of 2007 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal against the judgment and order dated 30.10.2006 passed by the Administrative. Tribunal-2, Dhaka in Administrative Tribunal Case No. 112 of 2005. The learned DAG submits that the present respondent No. 1 did not have any locus standi, right or interest to file the .appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and as such, the impugned judgment and order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in A.A.T Appeal No.  14 of 2007 is liable to be set aside. He further submits that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal passed the impugned judgment and order under misconception of both the judgments of the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 12 of 2003 and the provisions of Act XX of 2000.

5. Mr. Md. Nurul Islam, learned advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1, submits that the respondent No. 1 was prejudiced by the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal and as such, was legally entitled to prefer the appeal challenging the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal, which impinged upon her legal rights.

<u>6. The submissions made on behalf of the petitioner merit consideration. In such view of the matter, leave is granted to consider the following grounds:</u>

<u>I. Whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, was wrong in allowing the appeal having failed to appreciate that the learned Administrative Tribunal applying its judicial mind came to the lawful finding in favour of the necessity of preparing combined gradation list for promotion and hence the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.</u>

<u>II. Whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal made serious error of law in allowing the appeal while not considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the fact that the Administrative Tribunal directed the authorities to prepare combined gradation list following the provision of the direction of the Ministry of Establishment in the light of Act XX of 2000.</u>

7. The preparation of paper book is dispensed with as prayed for.

8. Let the operation or the judgment and order dated 04.07.2010 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in A.A.T. Appeal No. 14 of 2007 be stayed till disposal of the appeal.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 10, 2005 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 214 of 2005)
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin CJ: This petition for leave to appeal has been filed against the order dated July 10, 2005 (Order No.6 dated 10.7.2005) of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No. 214 of 2005.

2. The aforesaid appeal, as it appears, was filed against the judgment and order dated April 10, 2004 of the Administrative Tribunal, Chittagong in Administrative Tribunal Case No. 9 of 2003. The Administrative Tribunal by the aforesaid judgment and order allowed the case and thereupon set aside the order of dismissal of the respondent herein, petitioner before the Administrative Tribunal.

3. The Administrative Tribunal upon allowing the case passed the following “প্রাথীক চাকুরীতে পুনঃবহাল গণ্যে বিদ্যমান বিধির বিধান সাপ্যে যাবতীয় আর্থিক সুবিধাদি প্রাপক হইবেন”।

4. The case before the Administrative Tribunal was disposed of in presence of the parties to the case.

5. As against the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal in Administrative Tribunal Case, No. 9 of 2003, Government filed appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, being Appeal No. 214 of 2005.

<u>6. The appeal so filed was barred by time and as such an application for condonation of delay was filed.</u>

7. The delay in filing the appeal was 3 months and 16 days.

8. The appeal as per provision of section 6(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act was required to be filed within 3 (three) months from the date of judgment.

9. Section 6(2A) of the Administrative Tribunal Act provides for condonation of delay in case of failure to file an appeal against the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal within 3 (three) months but filed within 6 (six) months from the date of judgment and order, of the Administrative Tribunal i.e. within 3 (three) months on the expiry of the period for filing the appeal prescribed in section 6(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act.

10. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal noticed certain facts i.e. the date of delivery of judgment (10.4.2004), the date of filing application for obtaining the certified copy of the judgment and order (08.08.2004), date of putting the requisites for preparation of the certified copy of the judgment and order (12.08.2004), making the certified copy of the judgment and order ready for delivery (25.08.2004), taking delivery of the certified copy of the judgment and order (31.08.2004) and the date of filing of the appeal (24.11.2004).

11. In the background of the aforesaid facts the Administrative Appellate Tribunal observed "Even after exclusion of time consumed by the Tribunal in delivering the certified copy, the appeal has not been filed within 6 months from the date of the delivery of the judgment and as such the appeal is hopelessly time barred" and thereupon rejected the application for condonation of delay in filing the appeal and consequent thereupon dismissed the memo of appeal on the ground of limitation.

12. Facts as stated herein before relating to obtaining the certified copy for filing the appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal had not been disputed by the learned Deputy Attorney General.

13. The facts as have been reflected in the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal; clearly show that the appeal was filed beyond the period as provides in section 6(2A) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980.

14. The law as in the Act empowers the Administrative Appellate Tribunal to condone the delay in filing the appeal after the period prescribed in section 6(2) of the Act, if sufficiently explain. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal is competent to entertain an appeal upon condonation of delay, when sufficiently explained, only when the same is filed within 3 months from the date of expiry of the period prescribed in section 6(2) of the Act. From the reading of the law as in sections 6(2) and 6(2A) of the Administrative Tribunal Act we are of the view the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was not in error in refusing to entertain the Appeal No. 214 of 2005 since the same was filed beyond the period prescribed in section 6(2A) of the Administrative Tribunal Act. In a case, as in the instant one, inspite of offering explanation for not filing the appeal within the time prescribed by the law, as in section 6(2A) of the Act, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal is not competent to entertain an appeal on condonation of delay or in other words after expiry of the period as prescribes in section 6(2A) of the Act, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal is incompetent to entertain an appeal, although delay in filing   the appeal has been sufficiently explained. Explaining of delay in filing the appeal is limited to the period mentioned in Section 6(2A) of the Act and not beyond that.

<u>15. In our view the power of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal as regard condonation of delay is limited to a case which has been filed within 3 months after expiry of the period prescribes in section 6(2) of the Act and once the delay in filing the appeal is beyond the period as in section 6(2A) of the Act, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has no power to condone the delay inspite of offering sufficient explanation, which to the Tribunal may appear sufficient and satisfactory, as regard the delay since the Act has provided special period of limitation and once a case is beyond the said special period of the limitation the Court/Tribunal, herein the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, has no power to extend the period for filing the appeal on accepting of the explanation offered as regard the delay in filing the appeal, considering the same as sufficient and that merit of the case requires condonation of delay for doing justice to the parties.</u>

<u>16. It is the accepted principle of law that the justice is to be done evenly to the parties before the Court in a proceeding and not to one of the parties to the prejudice of the other when the party to whom justice has been done to the prejudice of the other was not vigilant and was guilty of latches and negligence and that special period of limitation has become effective and then the Court/Tribunal has no discretion to condone the delay upon ignoring the special period of limitation on resorting to the provision of section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908, or Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

17. Legislature prescribes period requiring one intends to approach a Court/tribunal to vindicate ones cause or grievance within the specified time for meaningful purpose i.e. for determination of any dispute apparent between the parties over any matter by the said specified time and thereby to give certainty regarding the subject matter of the dispute after a reasonable time. When prescribed period of limitation in pursuing a matter before the Court/Tribunal become effective against a party, he, thereby, has been debarred from pursuing his grievance upon resorting to a procedure prescribed for the redressed of such grievance and thereby the person against whom there is grievance saved from hassle at Court/Tribunal and is being freed from uncertainty.

18. Since the appeal filed by the petitioner herein was hopelessly time barred and the judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal being based on consideration of the facts which could not be shown incorrect from the side of the petitioners seeking leave to appeal, we find no reason to interfere with the order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal.

19. Accordingly, petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim J: The Civil Appeal Nos.143 and 144 of 2004 arising out of Civil Petition Nos. 1624 of 2003 and 688 of 2003 respectively by leave, are directed against the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 09.11.2003 passed in Writ Petition No. 5951 of 2003 disposing of the case against the impugned judgment and order dated 21.05.2003 in Writ Petition No.1978 of 2003 discharging the same. In both the writ petitions the vires of Sections 5 and 6 of Druta Bichar Tribunal Ain, 2002 was challenged together with the notifications issued under the said Act being SRO No. 233-Ain/2003 purporting to transfer Companigonj Police Station Case No.11 dated 12.08.2001 under Sections 147/148/149 /448/ 324/326/ 307/302/ 380/ 347/ 34 of the Penal Code corresponding to GR. Case No.1003 in Writ Petition No.5951 of 2003 and SRO No.38 Ain/2003 purporting to transfer Bandar Police Station Case No. 30 dated 19.04.1993 under Sections 147/148/149/302 of the Penal Code to Druta Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong in Well Petition No.1978 of 2003.

2. The Government of Bangladesh filed the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.36 of 2004 against the impugned direction in the judgment and order dated 09.11.2003 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.5951 of 2003 directing the writ respondents petitioners in the leave petition, to pass necessary order within 2(two) weeks from the date of receipt of the order for trial of the Companigonj Police Station Case No. 1 dated 12.08.2001 arising out of GR. Case No.1003 of 2001/Sessions Case No. 11 of 2003 by Druta Bichar Tribunal setting up at any place in the Headquarter at District Noakhali and if it is not done the writ-respondents were directed to modify/amended the notification dated 02.08.2003 (Annexure-B to the writ petition No.5951 of 2003) deleting the afore-said Companigonj Police Station Case No.11 dated 12.08.2001 appearing at serial No.79 of the list Annexure-B within 3(three) weeks from the date of receipt of the order. This Court granted leave in the aforesaid leave petition by the order dated 4th April, 2004 and thereupon Appeal No. 145 of 2004 was registered.

3. The writ petitioner in Writ Petition No.5951 of 2003 moved the High Court Division stating, inter-alia, that the petitioner is the elected Chairman of Basurhat Pourashava, Upazila-Companigonj, District Noakhali. He is the younger brother of former State Minister for Youth and Sports Affairs, Md. Obaidul Kader, who was elected as a Member of Parliament being nominated by Bangladesh Awami League in 1996. The petitioner and other accused persons worked in favour of Mr. Obaidul Karla, a nominated candidate of Bangladesh Awami League in the last parliamentary election held on October 01, 2001 and incurred anger and displeasure of the leaders of the ruling BNP-Jannat Four Party Alliance and because of satisfied against the writ petitioner under the provisions of Druto Bichar Tribunal Ain, 2002. Accordingly, the vires of Sections 5 and 6 of the Druta Bichar Tribunal Ain, 2002, (the Ain), have been challenged together with the notification being under S.RO. No.233-Ain/2003 dated 02.08.2003 issued under the said Ain as malafide, discriminatory, arbitrary and violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 32 and 35 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, and the same was issued with the ill motive and purpose to create scope to "pick and choose" policy against the accused for transferring Companigonj Police Station Case No.11 dated 12.08.2001 corresponding to G.R. No.1003 of 2001 to the Druta Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong from the Court of Additional Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Noakhali.

4. The facts leading to the case, as stated by the writ petition, are that on 12.08.2001 one Didarul Islam, son of Md. Mostafa, of Village Rampur, Police Station Companigonj, District Noakhali, a local leader of B.N.P. lodged an First Information Report with the Companigonj Police Station against 97 persons including the petitioner under Sections 147/148 /149 /324/ 326/ 307/ 302/379/427 of the Penal Code, alleging, inter-alia, that on12.082001 at about 9 a.m. while BNP leaders and workers were in a meeting in their party office, accused-persons being armed with fire arms attacked them and fired shots at them and consequently, one Alamgir died on the spot and 9 others were injured. Police upon a perfunctory investigation submitted charge sheet No.21 dated 26.02.2002 against 49 accused including the writ petitioner under Sections 147/148/149/448/324 /326/307/302/380/427/34 of the Penal Code. It was stated that after submission of charge sheet, the Cognizance Court No.3, Noakhali accepting the charge sheet taking cognizance sent the case record to the Court of Sessions Judge, Noakhali for trial and the learned Sessions Judge, Noakhali, transferred the case to the Court of Additional Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Noakhali for trial, where the case was pending for framing of charge. Meanwhile, Additional Sessions Judge also discharged 4 (four) accused persons from the case under Section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure by order dated 24.05.2003, fixing the date on 16.06.2003 for framing of charge and thereafter, it has been fixed on 26.08.2003 for framing of charge. All the accused hail from Companigonj Upazila, District Noakhali but the Government issued the notification for transferring the case to the Druta Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong with the malafide intention to harass and to deprive them of fair and impartial trial. Accused are very poor and some of them are physically very ill and are quite incapable to go to Chittagong from Companigonj, Noakhali to attend the Druta Bichar Tribunal, at Chittagong and the untold inconvenience, misery and the heavy costs in going to Chittagong and returning to Companigonj would be unbearable on the part of the accused petitioners and that would be repugnant to the scheme of fair trial guaranteed under Article 35 of the Constitution. It was stated that the Druta Bichar Tribunal AIN, 2002 (Act XX VIII of 2002) has been enacted on 1st December, 2002 with retrospective effect from 24th October, 2002. Instant case being Companigonj Police Station Case No.11 dated 12.08.2001 lodged on 12.08.2001, long before enactment of the impugned Act the instant case does not fall within the Ainbit of Section 1 of the Act, and there is no scope of giving retrospective effect for application of Act XXVIII of 2002 since the same has not been specifically provided for in the said Act. It was further stated in the writ petition that the State being a party in the case, it cannot and should not decide which sorts of cases would go to Druta Bichar Tribunal. The laws of the land should be uniform. One set of accused persons under the same sections within the jurisdiction cannot be tried by different Courts, and the matter is totally contrary to the provisions of Articles 27 and 31 of our Constitution. The provisions of Sections 5 and 6 of the Drina Bichar Tribunal Ain, 2002 confer unbridled and arbitrary power upon the Government to transfer case to Druta Bichar Tribunal under the said Act without recording any reason and without adhering to the principles of natural justice and there is no guideline in the Act, as to when and under what circumstances, this power of transfer could be exercised.

5. The leave petitioners in Civil Petition No.688 of 2003 stated that the subject-matter of the case under reference being S.T. Case No.542 of 1999 is under Sections 147/148/302 of the Penal Code pending in the Court of Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong corresponding to G.R. Case No.507 of 1993 arising out of the Bandar Police Station Case No. 30(4)1993 under Sections 147/148/149/302 of the Penal Code. The said criminal proceeding was in the process of trial in accordance with the provision of law of the land but due to the political connection of the informant the case has been listed in Gazette dated 5th February 2003 published by the respondents at the instance of present ruling party ignoring and disregarding the provisions   of the Constitution. Petitioners are facing the legal consequences of the case by way of facing the trial and enjoying the privilege of bail but respondents violating the Constitutional provision provided under Article 35 of the Constitution included the case in the list of Druto Bichar Tribunal case on the basis of the so-called power given under Druto Bichar Tribunal Act, 2002. The impugned Act was published in the additional gazette dated 24th October, 2002 and the impugned order of transferring the concerned criminal proceeding to Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong was published in the additional gazette dated 5th February, 2003. The impugned Act and the impugned order are violative of the fundamental right of equality before law guar-anteed by Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution, the fundamental right in respect of trial and punishment guaranteed under Article 35 of the Constitution, the impugned Act and order are also inconsistent with fundamental right and not sustainable in law and thereby liable to be declared void. The impugned Act and the order are also contrary to the provision of supremacy of the Constitution guaranteed by Article 7 of the Constitution. By way of passing of the impugned Act and issuing the impugned order the respondents acted contrary to the provision of right of life and personal liberty enshrined in the Constitution and as such the impugned Act and the impugned order of transfer are unconstitutional and void.

6. The High Court Division, however, upon hearing the Rule, disposed of the Rule in Writ Petition No. 5951 of 2003 with the direction as stated above and summarily rejected Writ Petition No. 6047 of 2003. The writ petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 5951 and 6047 of 2003 against the judgment of High Court Division filed Leave Petition Nos. 1624 and 688 of 2003 and the Government and others filed Leave Petition No. 36 of 2004 against direction in Writ Petition No. 5951 of 2003.

7. Besides these appeals, subject matter of respective civil petitions of all other cases have taken up together as the reasons involved therein are similar and accordingly, are taken up for hearing together and disposed of by this single judgment.

8. Leave was granted to consider the contention "Mr. A.F.M Hassan Arif the learned Attorney General of Bangladesh appearing for the petitioner in Civil Petition No.36 of 2004 submitted that an under trial prisoner is also entitled to get speedy trial without being languishing in jail without trial for an indefinite period and it is a fundamental right of an under trial prisoner to get speedy trial and thus the High Court Division erred in law in granting stay against the spirit of law and intention of the legislature in enacting the Act No.28 of 2002. The learned Attorney General further submitted that section 5 and 6 of the Act 28 of 2002 having been challenged in writ jurisdiction and the said two sections have been found to be the valid law and the decision to that effect has been reported in 55 DLR 636, as such, High Court Division ought not to have granted stay of proceedings while issuing the rule challenging the vices of certain provisions of the law.

9. The learned Attorney General further submitted that the High Court Division committed illegality in directing the Government to establish Druto Bichar Tribunal under sections 4 of the Druto Bichar Tribunal Act, 2002 inasmuch as the authority to establish forum for administrating the criminal justice lies with the Government both under section 9 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as well as under section 4 of the Druto Bichar Tribunal Act, XXVIII of 2002 and that thus has exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution of the; People's Republic of Bangladesh. The learned Attorney General submitted that the High Court Division committed illegality in directing to delete Companigonj Police Station Case No.11(8)01 appearing as item No.79 in the gazette notification under SRO No.33-Ain/2003 dated 2nd August, 2003 transferring the case to Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong in as-much as the High Court Division has itself having held the law regarding transfer to be valid one and not ultra-vires, the directions to delete i.e. thereby stopping transfer is not in conformity with the law as well as the judgment itself and the order of deletion is without jurisdiction.

10. Mr. Amirul-Islam, and Mr. Abdul Basel Majumder, learned Counsel appearing for the respondent submitted that Sections 5 and 6 of the Druto Bichar Tribunal Ain is ultra vires to the Constitution as it tends to destroy the fundamental structure of the Constitution allowing the executive authority to intrude into the area of judicial organ of the Republic including that of the High Court Division having exclusive domain as provided under Article 110 of the Constitution and Section 526 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to transfer a case pending before an ordinary Court of law, thereby destroying the balance of the Constitution violating the independence and separation of judiciary protected under the Constitution as basic structure of the same. The learned Counsel further submitted that the impugned 'Ain' and the order is violative of Article 110, read along with Article 35 and Article 22 allowing exclusive domain to transfer a pending case on the ground of general public importance. The learned Counsel submitted that the impugned AIN is violative of Article 27 read along with Articles 31, 32 and 35 of the Constitution. The learned Counsel further submitted that the impugned AIN in Sections 4, 5 and 6 are inherently discriminatory between the persons similarly situated allows the executive authority to exercise unfettered and unguarded discretion inasmuch as the Ain does not provide any guideline in determining and deciding which cases are to be transferred or not, nor provided any criteria and yardstick nor provides any transparent policy, a neutral board or independent authority making such determination, thereby arbitrary pick and choose leading to discriminatory application allowing the executive authority unfettered and unguarded exercise of discretion resulting in abuse of power which is inherent in the AIN itself The learned Counsel further submitted that there being no guideline as to geographical proximity, access to the Court specifying the area without any rational qualification or nexus leading to arbitrary exercise of power under the impugned AIN for formation of the Court under the impugned AIN, the formation of 6 Courts for the whole country only under Section 4 causes great hardship and harassment and the same is ultra-vires and violative of Article 116 of the Constitution."

11. Mr. Salahuddin Ahmed, learned Additional Attorney General, appearing for the appellants in Civil Appeal No.145 of 2004 submitted that an under trial prisoner is also entitled to get speedy trial without being languishing in jail without trial for an indefinite period and it is a fundamental right of an under-trial prisoner to get speedy trial and that the Act XXVIII of 2002 providing for speedy trial by Tribunal is legal and proper, that Sections 5 and 6 of the Act XXVIII of 2002 having been challenged in writ jurisdiction and the said two Sections have been found to be valid law and the decision to that effect has been reported in 55 DLR 636 and as such, the High Court Division ought not to have granted stay of proceedings while issuing the Rule challenging the vires of certain provisions of the law; that the High Court Division committed illegality in directing the Government to establish Druto Bichar Tribunal under Section 4 of the Druto Bichar Tribunal Act, 2002 inasmuch as the authority to establish forum for administrating the criminal justice lies with the Government both under Section 9 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as well as under Section 4 of the Druto Bichar Tribunal Act, XXVIII of 2002 and thus has exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution.

12. The learned Additional Attorney General submitted that the High Court a Division committed illegality in directing to delete Companigonj Police Station Case No.11(8)01 appearing as item No.79 in the Gazette Notification in SRO No.33- AIN 2003 dated 2nd August, 2003 transfer-ring the case to Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong inasmuch as the High Court Division has itself having held the law regarding transfer to be valid one and not ultra-vires, the directions to delete i.e. thereby stopping transfer is not in conformity with the law as well as the judgment itself and the order of deletion is without jurisdiction; that trial before a speedy tribunal is under the identical Code of Criminal Procedure as in a Court of Sessions trying Sessions cases by application of evidence act with right of appeal before identical appellate forum of the Supreme Court, the High Court Division had no speedy mode and manner of trial terminating in conviction, sentence or judgment or acquittal as the case may be and that in the purview of speedy tribunal's jurisdiction only specified nature of grave cases viz murder, rape, fire arms, narcotics are triable and that in such purview of jurisdiction said offences are tried in consonance with principles of natural justice guaranteeing right of fair trial under the existing law of dispensation of criminal justice by Court of Sessions without interference to a citizen's right to get fair trial as guaranteed under the Constitution.

13. The learned Additional Attorney further submitted that pursuant to the provision of Article 35(3) of the Constitution the accused having a right to speedy trial, the Government in its anxiety to arrange such speedy trial, enacted the law and that there is no bar in the Constitution in transferring any case to the Special Tribunal so formed by the AIN and that regarding the objection as to applicability of the Ain with retrospective effect; that there is no difference in the matter of awarding punishment and only the procedure being provided, the enactment giving its effect retrospectively for speedy trial and disposal of specified cases in the of justice cannot be regarded as a bad law. Referring to Section 6 of the Ain the learned Additional Attorney General submitted that there is sufficient guideline in making orders to transfer the cases inasmuch as the Government in the public interest may transfer cases of grave nature viz murder, rape, arms, explosive substance and drugs and as such, it cannot be said that there is no guideline in the Ain.

14. In order to appreciate the submissions we refer Sections 5 and 6 of the AIN which run as follows;

"৫. এখতিয়ার সরকার-সরকারী গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা যে মামলা দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনালে স্থানান্তর করিবে শুধু সেই মামলাই এই ট্রাইব্যুনালে বিচার করিবে।

৬. মামলা স্থানান্তর সরকার, সরকারী গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা জনস্বার্থে হত্যা, ধর্ষন, আগ্নেয়াস্ত্র, বিষ্ফোরক দ্রব্য এবং মাদকদ্রব্য সংক্রান্ত বিচারধীন কোন মামলা উহার যে কোন পর্যায়ে এমত, দায়রা আদালত বা বিশেষ আদালত বা ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেট আদালত হইতে বিচারের জন্য দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনালে স্থানান্তর করিতে পারিবে।”

15. It appears from aforesaid Section 5 of the Ain that the Tribunal shall hold trial under said Section only those cases mentioned in the Gazette Notification and the provision in Section 6 provides which cases would be transferred by the Government through Gazette Notification to the Tribunal established under the AIN. It is the concurrent finding of the High Court Division that there is prima-facie, no hide and sick or chooses and pick in making the transfer of the cases.

16. Now let us consider as to whether there is any foul observation or otherwise foul play in the matter of transfer of the cases or any guideline required for the purpose. In Section 6 it has been provided that the Government in the public interest by making notification in the Gazette may transfer the cases involving murder, rape, arms, explosive substance and drugs which are pending before the other Courts. It has been persistently submitted that the aforesaid provisions are violative of Article 27 of the Constitution. Article 27 of the Constitution runs as follows;

"27. All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law."

17. The High Court Division found that there is no major departure of the procedure of trial in the cases. Under Section 17 of the AIN it has been provided that provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure so far as they are not inconsistent with the provision of the Also shall apply to the proceeding of the Druto Bichar Tribunal, There are, of course, in Section 9 of the Ain, provisions for application of Chapter XX of the Code of Criminal Procedure in trial of the cases. On perusal of the provision of Chapter XX of the Code of Criminal Procedure the High Court Division did not find that as a result of holding trial under Chapter XX, in the interest of speedy trial of the cases pursuant to the principle of Article 35(3) of the Constitution, there is any chance of prejudice to the writ-petitioners.

18. After consideration of the provision of Article 35(3) of the Constitution providing for speedy trial of the criminal case and also after giving its anxious consideration to the submissions made by the learned Counsel of the appellants, the High Court Division is of the view that the impugned enactment and the provisions of Sections 5 and 6 thereof are not liable to be declared as ultra vires.

19. To obtain aim and object of the Ain, provision has been made in Section 4(4) of Druto 13ichar AIN, 2002 empowering Government to establish Tribunal(s) at place or places and the said provision is as under;

“৪. দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনাল স্থাপনঃ ৪ সরকার যে স্থান বা স্থানসমূহ নির্ধারণ করিবে সেই স্থানে বা স্থানসমূহের যে কোন স্থানে দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনাল বসিতে পারিবে এবং উহার কাযক্রম পরিচালনা করিতে পারিবে।”

20. Under the aforesaid provision the Druto Bichar Tribunal may sit and transact its proceeding at such place or places as the Government decides.

21. The broad facts of the case as submitted by the accused, are that the Sessions cases ripe for hearing upon framing of the ,charge and are usually fixed for hearing in the respective Sessions jurisdiction but issuing the notification in question transferring the cases to the Druto Bichar Tribunal to Chittagong for trial resorting to provisions of the Ain and resulting deprivation of fair and impartial trial in as-much as the movement of the accused beyond the jurisdiction would lead to unnecessary excess cost of transportation, lodging, finding lawyer and engaging of new lawyer in a Court beyond the jurisdiction would be not only costly but also difficult to provide instructions for the poor public litigants who are not only financially injured but physically jeopardized solely with the malafide intention to harms and deprive them of fair or impartial trial inasmuch as the accused would be frequently incapable to go to Chittagong from Companigonj, Noakhali a separate district far away from the Court to attend the Tribunal at Chittagong leading to untold miseries and inconveniences rather than the heavy costs on the part of the accused which would be repugnant to the scheme of Tribunal granted under Article 35 of the Constitution.

22. Though the Druto Bichar Tribunal AIN was enacted on the 1st December, 2002 giving retrospective effect from the 24th October, 2002 and the learned Counsel has further submitted that it is although the accused charged of the same section of the Penal Code are tried under the Druto Bichar Tribunal AIN, 2002 (Act, XXXVIII of 2002) but the certain other accused charged of the same offences are being tried in the Sessions Court, the list of the same in gazette dated 5th February, 2003 smack political connection of the inform-ant to the utter detriment of the accused is violative of the fundamental right of equality before the law guaranteed under Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution and the fundamental right in respect of trial, punishment guaranteed under the Article 35 of the Constitution. The alleged transfer, inconsistent thereof is accordingly not sustainable in law.

23. The object, intended and purpose of criminal jurisprudence is for expeditious disposal of cases in the matter of investigation, trial and prompt delivery of judgment which is in consonance with the provision of Article 35(3) of the Constitution providing that an accused of a criminal offence shall have the right to speedy and public trial by the defendant through an impartial Court or Tribunal established by law. The actual intent and purpose of the provisions besides other clement has provided for a right to a speedy trial and this right is enshrined in the said Article designed for Ameliorating the rigour of criminal trial to the detriment to the right of the accused for getting justice and this right is a right which has been preserved and protected and safeguard under the provision of law and the Constitution. Any violation of any form Amounts negation of justice and leading to hardship and suffering of the accused and expeditious disposal of criminal cases has been preserved demanding that the trial should not be unnecessarily prolonged for long and should not be conducted to the utter detriment of the parties and should be held expeditious through a speedy process least the accused is to neither languish in custody for long for no fault of him nor there should be delayed justice ultimately resulting in negation of justice.

24. The recent trend of delay in disposal of criminal cases has created havoc in the adjudication of justice depriving the parties to get fair and impartial justice within a reasonable time and thereby justice is denied due to pilling of huge cases awaiting   disposal and accumulation of cases of any particular category for long resulting in delay in disposal of cases and pilling of huge backlog of cases.

<u>25. Speedy trial is the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence and law never intended that this process of bringing the offender to book or justice in the case should be delayed or thus denying the parties to the litigant justice due to protracted litigation Amounting to denied of justice. Delayed justice also causes unnecessary obstruction in the smooth disposal of the case by the Court dispensing with justice.</u>

26. Section 6 of the Druto Bichar Tribunal AIN has made no stringent provision and there is no reason how the time limit for disposal of the case will affect the petitioner or change of venue from one place to another in respect of specified offences could affect the petitioner's right to trial in Court of law of competent jurisdiction for holding trial thereof. In our Constitution Article 35(3) clearly provides for that a person accused of criminal offence shall have the right to have the speedy trial in consonance with the said provision of law and the age old practice of disposal of Sessions cases in our Country in session within a very shot space of time has been reiterated in Druto Bichar Tribunal Ain keeping intact practice and procedure and principle of trial of the cases of the nature as specified in the said Ain.

27. If we consider the provision regarding equality before the law or equal protection under the law, we find that in the instant cases there are sufficient guidelines in the AIN so as to which classes of cases of the offenders are triable by the Tribunal. Scrutinising the provision laid down in Druto Bichar AIN we do not find that there was any chance of discrimination or legislature made no discriminatory treatment in respect of the same specified offences. The provision made in the AIN in Sections 5 and 6 thereof provides for trial of specified cases by Druto Bichar Tribunal upon transfer of pending cases of the nature from the Court of the learned Sessions Judges set up for speedy trial in six Divisions of the Country. It is true to be submitted that procedure for trial followed for the normal Court of Sessions jurisdiction are specifically the same in the Druto Bichar Tribunal. The transfer of the cases of the nature specified in the Ain have no chance of adversely affecting or prejudicing the accused but aim and object of the said AIN was for disposal of the cases within a reasonable promptitude and/or very shortest possible time in order to avoid any delay in disposal causing mischievous of justice to the accused. The purpose of the Ain is to ensure speedy trial in keeping with the aforesaid provision and law and the practice and procedure of the Court since not being adhered to recently due to the filing of good number of various types of cases in the Sessions Court keeping in view with the universally accepted principle of providing speedy trial to the accused.

28. Section 5 quoted above specified the types of cases to be tried by the Tribunal and Section 6 specifically provides for offences of murder, rape, firearms, explosive substances and drugs may be transferred by the Government in the public interest by way of notification in the gazette from the Court of Sessions or Special Court or of a Court of Magistrate as the case may be. The Ain, in our view, does not in any way affect the right of the accused far less offending any fundamental right of the accused because Section 7 specifically provides that the Tribunal shall be deemed to be Court of Sessions and the provision of the Ain shall apply in respect of the trial of the cases before the Tribunal.

29. On perusal of the said provision of impugned AIN in juxtaposition with the normal law of the land we do not find that any right of the accused has been curtailed to get a free, fair and impartial trial before a Tribunal.

30. Druto Bichar Tribunal Ain, 2002 provides for the purpose and intent of framing the law; যেহেতু কতিপয় অপরাধের ত্বরিত বিচারের জন্য দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনাল স্থাপন করা সমীচীন ও প্রয়োজনীয় and accordingly the said Ain has provided provision to set up Druto Bichar Tribunal for speedy trial of certain offences.

31. Certain provisions of Druto Bichar Tribunal Ain, 2002 namely, Section 7,8 and 9 are required to be examined as to whether the same provide for any other procedure for trial of the specified Sessions cases before the Druto Bichar Tribunal.

32. Section 7 of the Ain provides that “৭। (১) দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনাল একটি দায়রা আদালত বলিয়া গন্য হইবে।

(২) দ্রুত বিচার ট্রাইব্যুনাল তৎকর্তৃক বিচারকৃত অপরাধের জন্য সংশ্লিষ্ট আইন দ্বারা নির্ধারিত যে কোন দন্ড আরোপ করিতে পারিবে।

33. Sub-section (1) of Section 7 provides that the Druto Bichar Tribunal shall deem to be a Sessions Court; Sub-section (2) of Section 7 provides that Druto Bichar Tribunal could impose any penalty/sentence for the offences specified in the concerned parent Acts. Thus, from the above, we find that the said Tribunal has the power and jurisdiction of a Sessions Court to deal with the accused in the manner provided by the concerned Act i.e. Code Tribunal of Criminal Procedure and Penal Code.

34. Section 8 speaks of the trial of the cases; sub-section (1) provides that Druto Bichar Tribunal shall try a case from the stage of the case was pending before the Sessions Court. Sub-section (2) thereof provides that the deposition of the witnesses before the Sessions Court upon transfer to the Tribunal shall be treated to be the deposition before the Tribunal and the Tribunal could in the interest of justice as necessary take evidence afresh. Thus, there is no change in any trial procedure before the Tribunal upon transfer of the case to the Druto Bichar Tribunal.

35. Section 9 provides that the cases since transferred to the Druto Bichar Tribunal shall be carried out following Chapter XX of the Code of Criminal Procedure as far as practicable. Sub-section (2) of Section 9 provides that cases shall be conducted in a summary procedure unless the punishment of any offences of death penalty, imprisonment for life or more than 7 years in that case the provision of Chapter XXII of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall be followed. An accused enlarged on bail by the Sessions Court upon transfer of the case to the Druto Bichar Tribunal could apply for enlargement on bail and the Tribunal shall dispose of the same following the provision applicable for the offences.

<u>36. Apart from above, Section 10 has provided for the time limit for completing the disposal of the case. From the above it is crystal clear that the transfer of the case to Druto Bichar Tribunal has in no way affected the right of the parties as provided in the Code of Criminal Procedure excepting the time frame within which the trial has to be completed keeping the view of the spirit of the criminal jurisprudence and a normal practice and procedure that any delinquent entitled to speedy dispose of the case instead of lingering the same for years together in order to secure the ends of justice.</u>

37. Moreover, the AIN provides a guiding principle taking the provisions in the Ain as a whole which does not affect the right and obligation of the parties in application of the special provision to specified cases of offences mentioned in the AIN inasmuch as we find nexus both the offences of a particular category and the object with which the AIN was promulgated. In that view of the matter the allegation of discrimination is of no avail as there are sufficient justifications of the introduction of Druto Bichar Tribunal AIN for specified offences and for speedier trial of those offences. In that view of the matter we can profitably quote a passage from the decision in the case of Kathi Raning-vs-State of Saurashtra reported in AIR 1952 SC 123 which answered the justifi ability of such law and nullified the allegation of `choose and pick' of any particular cases to be tried in the said Tribunal as under;

"The Ordinance, as I have already stated, purported to amend another Ordinance, the objection which was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquility in the State. It was not disputed before us that the preamble of the original Ordinance would govern the Amending Ordinance also, and the object of promulgating the subsequent Ordinance was the same as the object of promulgating the original Ordinance. Once this is appreciated, it is easy to see that there is something in the Ordinance itself to guide the State Government to apply the special procedure not to any and every case but only to those cases or offences which have relation to or connection with the main object and purpose of the Ordinance and which for that reason become a class by themselves requiring to be dealt with on a special footing. The clear recital of a definite objective furnishes a tangible and rational basis of classification to the State Government for the purpose of applying the provisions of the Ordinance and for choosing only such offence or cases as affect public safety,   maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquility. Thus, the State is expected to select only such offences or classes of offences or class of cases for being tried by the special Court in accordance with the special procedure, as are calculated to affect public safety, maintenance of public order, etc, and the use of the special procedure must necessarily be confined to only disturbed areas or those areas were adoption of public safety measures in necessary."

<u>38. In that view of the matter we are of the view that the equal protection clause of the Constitution has not been violated as the Ain is in respect of the offences specified therein and as such, the classification of the said offences is not arbitrary or caprice but bearing a reasonable relation with the objective which the legislation has in view.</u>

39. Section 6 of the AIN refers to five distinct categories of offences/classes of offences empowering the Government to direct any one or more of cases, offences to be tried by Druto Bichar Tribunal under the Ain. The specified offences, prima-facie, do not contemplate any particular offender or any particular accused in any particular cases. The emphasis is on 'offence' or 'offences' and not in any way calculated to touch any particular accused. Such classification does not refer to or is not directed towards singling out of any particular person or any particular offences but is directed against the offences, group of the offences or classes of offences or classes of cases mentioned in the said provision of Section 5. In that view of the matter it is of no merit to argue that the AIN is designed to pick and choose of any particular offences or any particular accused.

40. The provision of Druto Bichar AIN has been thoroughly dealt with in the case of Muhibur Rahman Manik and others-vs-Bangladesh and others reported in 55 DLR 636 and the issues raised therein were also agitated therein and decided by the learned Judges and set at rest in the said illuminating judgment with which we have no reason to differ or to depart from.

<u>41. Sections 5 and 6 of the Ain read together do not either in terms of necessary implication discriminate both a person or classes of persons or purport to deny to any one equality before law or equal protection of law because the Ain does not make any such law derogatory to the aforesaid principle as the AIN is applicable to the trial of offences or classes of offences or classes of cases. Keeping in view the constitutional provision as provides under Article 35(3), thus, by no stretch of imagination it could be alleged any discriminatory intent on the part of the Government because there is no departure Appellate Division Cases from the normal procedure excepting that (Civil) the cases regarding certain categories of cases specified in Section 6 to be transferred to the Tribunal for expeditious disposal of the same. Even if discretion could be alleged in such offences or classes of offences or classes of cases as the case may be but the main object is for speedier trial exercised by the Government in exercise of its duty for providing speedy trial of the cases.</u>

42. In view of the above C.A. Nos.143 and 144 of 2004 are hereby dismissed and C.A. No.145 of 2004 is allowed. Accordingly, in the light of the discussion and finding regarding the validity of the Ain itself and on the principle of law made in the body of the judgment and all the C.P s are accordingly dismissed and the Druto Bichar Tribunal are directed to dispose of the aforesaid respective cases speedily and in accordance with law.

End.
