case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated March 29, 1998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2248 of 1991 (Dhaka)Civil Revision No. 271 of 1984 (Rangpur) )
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J:- The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have filed, by leave, the instant appeal against the judgment dated March 29, 1998 by the High Court Division in in Civil Revision No. 2248 of 1991 (Dhaka)Civil Revision No. 271 of 1984 (Rangpur) making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated July, 19, 1984 of the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Nawabganj in Title Appeal No. 176 of 1982 reversing the judgment and decree dated April 30, 1982 of the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Nawabganj in Other Class Suit No. 28 of 1977 decreeing the same.

<u>2. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title and khas possession upon evicting the defendants from the land in suit.</u>

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the land in suit, which is homestead, belonged to Jairuddin and in his name C.S. record was prepared, that said Jairuddin died leaving daughter Araben Nessa and nephew (brother's son) Giasuddin and they inherited the land left by Jairuddin including the suit land, that Jairuddin used to possess the land through pargadar, that S. A. record was prepare in the name of Jairuddin that Araben Nessa and Lokman son of Giasauddin transferred the land in suit to the plaintiff by the kabala dated January 19, 1970 and since then plaintiff is possessing the land on payment of rent to the Government that there is passage over the suit plot No. 837 and the said path has divided the land of plot No. 837 in two parts, in one part .03 decimal of land, that recent revisional record of right has been prepared in respect of 13 decimals of land in the name of the plaintiff, that the defendants upon claiming the land in suit on the basis of the kabala dated November 25, 1976 obtained from successive heirs of Jitu Mondal dispossessed the plaintiff from the `Kha' schedule land.

4. The case was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating inter alia, that Jairuddin was korfa tenant under Kuran Mondal in respect of the land of C. S khatian no. 409 of Mouza Rajarampur, that Jairuddin surrendered his korfa tenancy by a 'Istafanama' in 1335 B. S in favour of Kuran Mondal, that Kuran Mondal died leaving son Tarash Halder (Mondol) and made settlement of 10 decimals of land out of 15 decimals of land of plot No. 837 to Jitu Mondal by the 'Hukumnama' dated 9th Poush, 1345 B. S. and that on obtaining the settlement Jitu Mondal enjoyed the land so taken settlement by goring crops and that also paid rent, that Jitu Mondal died leaving 2 sons, 2 daughters, and by amicable partition amongst the said persons Jitu Mondal's son Gudar Ali relinquished his right in respect of the land of plot No. 837, that Jitu Mondal's one son and one daughter sold their share to their brother Alfazuddin and thus he became owner of 10 decimals of land, that 5 decimals of land was settled by Tares Mondal to Refatullah Mondal on the Magh, 1347 B. S. and he transferred the said land by oral gift to his wife Nayjan Nessa and mutated her name and paid rent, that Taresh Halder transferred the rent receiving interest to one Maniruddin Biswas by the deeds dated February 15, 1943 and 28.4.1943, that during S. A. operation land was recorded wrongly in the name of Jairuddin, the defendants are claiming the land in suit by purchase from the successive heirs of Jitu Mondal.

5. The trial Court decreed the suit on the findings that plaintiff proved his case of possessing the land in suit by bargadar by the evidence of P. Ws. 2 and 3, that no 'Istafanama' as well as no 'Hukumnama' was filed to prove surrender of possession by Jairuddin and settlement infavour of Jitu Mondal, that plaintiff in support of claim of payment of rent the Government has filed the Exts. 2-2 (c). that defendants tried to establish through D. W. 2 their case of surrender by Jairuddin but his evidence was here say evidence, that D. Ws. 1 and 2 have failed to prove that Jairuddin surrendered his tenancy in favour of Kuran Mondal, that no paper including Hukumnama has been filed to show 5 decimals of land was settled in favour of Refatullah, that the dakhilas Exts. C-C(2) filed to prove the case of settlement from Taresh Halder are concocted and fabricated papers, that Ext. B i.e. the kabala by which rent receiving interest was sold is in respect of plot No. 836 which is not a suit plot, that P. W. 4 neighbor of the plaintiff has deposed that Jairuddin had homestead in the land in suit, that P.Ws. have deposed that Jairuddin was the owner of the land in suit and that he used to possess the same through bargadar, that the plaintiff has got right, title and possession in the land in suit and that defendants dispossessed her. The trial Court also held that the suit as framed is quite maintainable and that for barred by limitation and also not bad for defect of party.

6. The defendant went on appeal. The appellate Court primarily placing reliance on the Ext. B and B (8) i. e. kabalas by Kuran Mondal's son Taresh Halder selling the rent receiving interest on 15.2.1943 and 28.4.1943 infavour of one Maniruddin held that those 2 documents 'are sufficient' to prove the surrender of the suit land by Jairuddin to Kuran Mondal. The appellate Court considered those 2 documents as the sufficient material to prove the case of surrender by Jairuddin since his name did not appear in the said 2 documents and thereupon held that neither Jaridudin for his heirs were the owners of the suit land but Faizuddin and Rafatullah were the actual owner" of the land in suit. The appellate Court was of the view that the learned Munsif decreed the suit without taking into consideration those 2 documents and the appellate Court was of the view that defendants "were the bonafide purchaser for consideration from the rightful owners" i. e. Refatullah and Faizuddin, the appellate Court though found substances in the contention of the plaintiff respondent that defendants have neither proved by oral evidence nor by filing `Istafanama' and Hukumnama' to establish their case of surrender by Jairuddin but held that non-production of those documents and that absence of oral evidence do not go to show that the Exts. B and B (8) are not genuine and that the said documents being genuine are sufficient to prove the fact of surrender by Jairdudin of his korfa tenancy in favour of Kuran Mondal under whom Jairuddin was the korfe tenant. On the aforesaid findings the appellate court set aside the judgment of the trial Court.

7. The plaintiff then moved the High Court Division in revisinal jurisdiction and obtained Rule in civil revision number as mentioned hereinbefore.

8. The High Court Division on the finding that neither the 'Istafanama' nor the 'Hukumnama' was produced from the side of the defendants, that defendants' claim of surrendering of korfa tenancy by Jairuddin has not been established upon leading evidence, oral and documentary, that defendants did not prove surrender by korfa tenancy by Jairuddin, nor proved the settlement by Kuran Mondal or Taresh Halder son of Kuran Mondal, that plaintiff proved his right, title, interest and possession in their land in suit and dispossession by the defendants from the land in suit by reliable oral evidence, that the finding on the basis of which trial Court decreed the suit were not reversed by the appellate court, that defendants alleged case of surrender of korfa tenancy by Jairdudin has not been established by legal evidence and that evidence, both oral and documentary, to that effect is lacking, that S. A record in the name of Alfajuddin and Rafatullah was prepared wrongly since tenancy of Jairuddin was not surrendered at any point of time in favour of kuran Modnal. Finally the High Court Division held that question of surrender by Jairdudin in favour of Kuran Mondal could not be established by the defendants and as such their claim in respect of the land in suit was not legal and they illegally dispossessed the plaintiff.

9. It may be mentioned trial Court on consideration of the oral evidence arrived at the finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the land in suit and he was dispossessed therefrom by the defendants. The plaintiff led evidence to prove his mode of possession through the bargadar. It was the case of the plaintiff that his bargadar planted bamboo in the land in suit. The appellate Court disbelieved this version of the plaintiff's case which was proved by reliable evidence, upon observing "Bamboo cultivation through the Bargadar is unknown and not in practical practice of this country. So, this facts cannot be believed". The fact of bamboo plantation in the land in suit finds support from the evidence of D.Ws. 2 and 3. It may also be mentioned the appellate Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court solely placing reliance on the Exts. B and B (8) whereby Taresh Mondal son of Kuran Mondal sold the rent receiving interest to certain Moniruddin as because in the said documents name of Jairuddin ws absent and thereupon was of the view had Jairuddin been the tenant of Kuran Months or for that matter Thresh Mondal his name would certainly have been in the said documents and that absence of Jairuddin's name in the said documents proved defendants case of surrender of tenancy by Jairuddin in favour of Kuran Mondal. The trial Court on consideration of the oral evidence along with the documentary evidence i.e. S.A. and R.S. record as well as Exts. 2-2 (c) rent receipts arrived at a finding that the plaintiff has right, title and interest in the land in suit and she was disposed from the land in suit. The appellate Court did not at all consider the oral evidence of the parties. The defendants tried to prove their case of 'Istafanama' by Jairuddin in favour of Kuran Mondal by the evidence of D.W.2. The trial Court discarded the evidence of said witness being here say one. On our scrutiny of the evidence of D.W.2 we find the evidence of the said witness hit by the rule of here say and as such we are of the view trial Court has rightly left out of consideration the evidence of D.W.2 We also find evidence of D.W.2 contradictory. The Defendants tried to prove their case of settlement by Taresh Mondal alias Taresh Halder son of Kuran Mondal alias Kuran Halder through the evidence of D.W.3 who is nephew of Jitu Mondal, the alleged settlement holder. The witness has stated that he is unable to say the date and the year of settlement by Taresh Mondal. It may be mentioned the defendants in support of their case of taking settlement from Taresh put into evidence dakhilas Exts. C-C (2). The trial Court on scrutiny of the said dakhilas held that the same were fictitious and concocted. The appellate Court did not at all addressed itself to this aspect of the case of the defendants because of which trial Court disbelieved the defendants claim of taking settlement of the land in suit from in suit from Taresh Mondal.

10. Leave was granted to consider the contention that in view of the fact that the plaintiff claimed her interest in the land in suit on the basis of purchase made on 19.01.1970 from successors-in-interest of the original tenant Jairuddin and the defendants contested the said claim on the basis of their purchase on 25.11.1976 from the heirs of Jitu Mondal who entered upon and possessed the land in suit in pursuance of surrender by Jairuddin of his korfa tenancy in respect of the land in suit to Kuran Mondal, the original owner, the real question is whether there was surrender by Jairuddin to Kuran Mondal the appellate Court having dismissed the suit on consideration of the Exts. B and B(8) which proved that the plaintiff's predecessor-in-interest surrendered the suit land to Kuran Mondal but the High Court Division acted illegally in setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court without considering that Exts. B and B(8) which are of about 4 years old on which the lower appellate Court relied for setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

11. The learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that evidence of D.Ws.2 and 3 read with Exts. B and B (8) sufficiently proved the fact of surrender by Jitu Mondal to Kuran Mondal and thereafter settlement to Jitu Mondal and possession of Jitu Mondal that had Exts. B and B(8) would have taken into consideration by the trial Court and the High Court Division the judgment would not have been the one as given by the trial Court and the High Court Division, that issue in the suit was required to be considered taking into consideration Ext. B and B(8) and the oral evidence of D.Ws. 2 and 3 but the trial Court and the High Court Division did not take the same into consideration while decreeing the suit and reversing the judgment of the appellate Court respectively, that High . Court Division set aside the judgment of the appellate court without consideration of the material evidence i.e. material evidence Exts. B and B(8) wherein there were mention of the names of korfa tenants but name of Jairuddin was absent and the said fact proved that he surrender his tenancy and had be not surrendered his tenancy his name would have found place in Exts. B and B (8) and that fact of settlement of the land in suit to Jitu Mondal finds support because of the presence of his name in Exts. B and B (8), that Exts. B and B (8) are of being more than 4 years old there is presumption of 'correctness those of.

<u>12. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Counsel of the appellant the learned Counsel for the Respondent No.1 submitted that in the leave granting order the real question for determination was correctly set forth i.e. whether there was surrender by Jairuddin of his korfa tenancy to the original owner Kuran Mondal and the said material fact was addressed by the trial Court and the High Court Division upon referring to the evidence, both oral and documentary and thereupon arrived at the finding that there was no surrender of korfa tenancy by Jairuddin to Kuran Mondal. The learned Counsel has also submitted that the Exts. B and B(8) having not been brought before the Court from the proper custody and that the contents thereof having not been proved and that the presumption of correctness of the said two documents being of more than 30 years old having been rebutted by the plaintiff by proving their possession of the land and preparation of record of right and payment of rent to the Government, the appellate Court merely placing reliance on those two document without considering the oral evidence as well as other documentary evidence at all and that without reversing the reasoning and the finding of the trial Court while discarding Exts. C-C (2) which were filed by the defendants in support of their case of taking settlement of the land in suit and that without reversing and setting aside the finding of the trial Court in discarding the evidence of D.W.2 through whom the defendants tried to prove their case of surrender of the tenancy by Jairuddin to Kuran Mondal and the evidence of D.W.3, though, whom defendants tried to establish their case taking settlement of the land in suit and that also without considering the fact of non-filing of Istafanama by Jairuddin and Hukumnama relating to settlement to Jitu Mondal and that without considering the oral evidence at all set aside the judgment of the trial Court an as the High Court Division on due consideration of the materials on record set aside the judgment of the appellate Court no interference is called for by this Court. The learned Counsel also submitted that the S.A. and the R.S. record were prepared in the name of plaintiff's vendor as well as in her name and in support thereof Exts. 2-2(C) having been produced, the same along with oral evidence clearly proved possession of the plaintiff. It has lastly been submitted by the learned Counsel that possession of the plaintiff and the defendants case of surrender of the tenancy by the plaintiff's predecessor Jairuddin in the background of the evidence on record as cannot go together the High Court Division as well as the trial Court were quite correct in finding the right, title and possession in favour of the plaintiff and that also in arriving at the finding that the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff from the land in suit.</u>

<u>13. The appellants for the purpose of establishing their case of surrender of korfa tenancy by Jairuddin in favour of Kuran Mondal and settlement of the land so surrendered by Jairuddin to Jitu Mondal primarily placed reliance on Exts. B and B(8) as well as on the evidence of D.Ws. 2 and 3. It has been submitted that had Jairuddin been a tenant under Kuran Mondal his name would have found place in Exts. B and B (8) and his name being not in the said exhibits it can be concluded that Jairuddin surrendered his tenancy in 1335 B.S. The submissions so made at the first instance appears to be plausible one but on scrutiny of the materials on record i.e. oral evidence as well as documentary evidence led from the side of the plaintiff showing preparation of the S.A. and R.S. record in the name of the plaintiff's predecessor in interest and in her name respectively and payment of rent by the plaintiff and of his being in possession of the land in suit and dispossession there form by the defendants clearly established that plaintiff's predecessor in interest Jairuddin did not surrender his tenancy and that he owned and possessed the land in suit and thereupon Jairuddin's heirs sold the land in suit to the plaintiff. From the defendants side it has been asserted that Jairuddin surrendered the tenancy by 'Istafanama' and that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as well as another got the settlement of the land so surrendered by Jairuddin by 'Hukumnama' None of the said documents were brought on record from the side of the defendants. The defendants i.e. the appellants tried to prove the matter of 'Istafanama' by Jairuddin through the evidence of D.W. 2. As already stated herein-before his evidence being here say is not legal evidence to establish defendants case of 'Istafanama' by Jairuddin. The appellants tried to establish their case of settlement through the evidence of D.W. 3. It has also been mentioned hereinbefore that he is not a disinterested witness, rather interested witness being nephew of Jitu Mondal through whom the defendants are claiming the land in suit nature and quality of evidence of D.W.3 has been discussed herein-above and as such his evidence cannot be considered worthy of making conclusion that land in suit was settled with Jitu Mondal on being surrendered by Jairuddin.</u>

14. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel of the appellants that the Exts. B and B (2) being the documents of 30 years old have presumption of correctness. The said submission has been made to substantiate the contention that had at the time of registration the contention that had at the time of registration of the aid documents i.e. Exts. B and B (8) whereby rent receiving interest was sold by Taresh Halder to one Moniruddin, Jairuddin had been korfa tenant of Kuran Mondal the name of Jairuddin would have certainly there. The presumption of correctness of the fact stated in the document is rebuttable one. The plaintiff by oral as well as documentary evidence has established his case that Jairuddin was a korfa tenant of Kuran Mondal and on the death of Jairuddin the land owned by him as korfa tenant devolved upon his dauthter Araben Nessa and his nephew Giasuddin who died leaving son Lokman and they i. e Araben Nessa and Lokman sold the land in 1970 to him. It may be mentioned S.A. record was prepared in the name of Jairuddin and R.S. record was prepared in the name of the plaintiff and he paid rent of the land so recorded in his name by Exts. 2-2 (c). As against the said state of the matter it was the case of the defendants that S.A. record was wrongly prepared in the name of Jairuddun.

15. On consideration of the materials on record particularly evidence as to possession of the land in suit by the plaintiff and before that by the heirs of Jairuddin in our view the contention that the S.A. record was wrongly prepared in the name of Jairuddin is not legally sustainable. The R. S. record has been prepared in the name of the plaintiff and she paid rent as mentioned hereinbefore. Since possession of the land in suit was with Jairuddin and thereafter land in suit is possessed by the plaintiff, as such it can readily be not concluded that since name of Jairuddin does not appear in the Exts. B and B (8) he surrendered his korfa tenancy in favour of Kuran Mondal. Since the defendants alleged that Jairuddin surrendered his tenancy under Kuran Mondal and thereafter Taresh son of Kuran Mondal settled the land with Jitu Mondal it was for the defendants to establish the said facts since in the absence of non-establishing of the said facts i.e. case of surrender and the settlement with Jitu Mondal the logical conclusion is that, that Jairuddin did not surrender his korfa tenancy in favour of Kuran Mondal.

16. The defendants tried to establish their case of settlement by producing rent receipt Exts. C-C (2). The trial Court on scrutiny of the same arrived at the finding that the said exhibits are concocted and spurious and the same have been brought into existence for the purpose of the instant case. In fact had the land been surrendered by Jairuddin to Juran Mondal and that had the same would have been settled with Jitu Mondal in 1345 B.S. the settlement holder i.e. Jitu Mondal had certainly paid rent to Taresh Mondal but no material has been brought in that regard. In the background of the materials brought on record by the plaintiff we are of the view that Jairuddin at no point of time surrendered his korfa tenancy and that on his death the land in suit was inherited by his daughter and nephew and after death of Jairuddin's nephew, his son Lokman inherited and the plaintiff by purchase from Jairuddin's daughter and Lokman has acquired right, title and interest in the land in suit and he was dispossessed from the land in suit by the defendants.

17. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we are of the view that High Court Division though have not considered the issue involved in the suit i.e. whether there was surrender by Jairuddin his korfa tenancy to Kuran Mondal under whom he was a korfa tenant elaborately but for that it cannot be said that High Court Division while setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court did not consider the material evidence. We find from the judgment under appeal the said Division in fact considered the issue involved in the suit i.e. the question of surrender by Jitu Mondal in favour of Kuran Mondal and in the background of the materials on record held that appellate Court did not advert to the findings and decisions of the trial Court and thereupon did not reverse the finding of the trial Court based on evidence. In our view High Court Division was not in error in holding that from the defendants' side evidence was lacking to establish the case of surrender by Jairuddin in favour of Kuran Mondal.

18. Since case of surrender of tenancy by Jairuddin was not established and that as in the background of the materials on record it cannot be said that merely because name of Jairuddin is absent in the Exts. B. and B (8) there would be a presumption that he surrendered his tenancy to Kuran Mondal and that as it has been established by the plaintiff that Jairuddin did not surrender his tenancy, we find no merit in the appeal.

Accordingly the appeal is dismissed with cost of Tk. 2,000/-

End.

lawyer:
M Hafizullah with Md Al-Amin Sarker and Md Ohiullah, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
No one appears—For the Respondents
parties:
Seacom Shipping Ltd ------ Petitioner 
Vs 
President, Customs, Excise & VAT Appellate Tribunal, Internal Resources Division and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J: Rule was issued upon the respondents to show cause why the impugned Order No. 3 dated 4-1-95 passed by the Custom Excise, VAT Appellate Tribunal on an appeal preferred by the writ petitioner-Company registered as file No. II-177/MCD/92/85/Cus arising out of appeal Order No. 87/1997 dated 29-4-97 passed by the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) rejecting the appeal, evidenced by Annexure-L the writ petition should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 
2. The respondents did not enter appearance and the Rule is not opposed. 
3. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner is the local shipping agent of the vessel MT Jamac of Liberia, which carried Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) in bulk for Bangladesh and that on arrival of the cargo at the Port of Chittagong a cargo manifest was submitted showing 17,150 metric tons of CDSO as the cargo carried for Bangladesh and that the quantity was surveyed on 24-8-92 at Chittagong Port under Ullage Survey method by an approved surveyor on board the vessel and the quantity was found at 17,049.57 metric tons and accordingly the difference between the declared manifested quantity of 17,150 metric tons and the Ullage Surveyed quantity of 17,049.57 metric tons was found to be 100.43 metric tons which was less than 1% of the difference allowed as Ocean allowance and that thereafter, the CDSO was discharged from the vessel to the shore tanks and accordingly, dry tanks certificate was issued by the Master of the vessel as by the surveyor certifying that the entire CDSO carried for Bangladesh Port has been discharged from the vessel and that thereafter another survey was conducted by dip reading of the shore tanks and a shortage of 236.709 metric tons was found on the basis of difference between the manifest declared quantity and the shore tank survey. report and accordingly, the Assistant Commissioner of Customs asked the petitioner to show cause about such shortage, to which the petitioner duly replied explaining the position denying their liabilities but the Adjudication Officer (respondent No. 7) without considering the Ullage Survey report and the dry tanks certificate imposed penalty of Taka 42,50,989.50 for the alleged shortage of 236.709 metric tons of CDSO relying on the shore tank survey report vide order dated 5-3-98 and being aggrieved there against the petitioner preferred Appeal under section 193 of the Chairman Act before the respondent No. 2, who upheld the order of the respondent No. 3 in part vide order No. 87/97 dated 29-4-97 reducing the penalty amount from Taka 42,50,989.50 to Taka 25,25,593. Being aggrieved the petitioner there- after preferred appeal there against before the respondent No. 1 Tribunal and the respondent No. 1 passed the impugned order dated 5-3-98 upholding the order passed by the respondent No. 2. The Appellate Tribunal erred in misreading the provisions of item No. 24(ii) of the table of section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 to the effect that any shortage, as to the quantity, which has to be found in the conveyance, if cannot be accounted for to the satisfaction of the Customs authority, the carrier will be liable under the said provisions and that the Appellate Tribunal failed to consider the fact that, declared manifested quantity was 17,150 metric tons of CDSO imported for Bangladesh and as per Ullage Survey the quantity was found to be 17,049.57 metric tons thereby, there was a shortage of 100.43 metric tons, which quantity was less than 1% comparing to the total quantity of 17,150 metric tons and 1% of shortage is within permissible limit as Ocean allowance and that the quantity of CDSO carried for Bangladesh Port as per Ullage Survey at the port of loading was 17063.52 metric tons and therefore, the actual shortage is (17,063.52-17,049.57) metric tons i.e. 13.95 metric tons, both measured under Ullage Survey method, and which is less than the permissible limit. 
4. Mr M Hafizullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner-company, submitted that the impugned order is bad both on fact as well as on law. The learned Advocate taking us to the relevant provisions of the Customs Act, 1969 as to the alleged offence, which is item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) relevant portion of which is quoted herein below: 
"If the quantity found in the conveyance is short, and the shortage is not accounted for to the satisfaction of the Officer-in-Charge of the Customs House." 
5. Submitted that in the instant case the purpose of shortage, 1% of the imported quantity carried by the vessel is allowed as Ocean allowance must be taken into account, and that the admitted position is that as per declared manifest the quantity imported for Bangladesh was 17,150 metric tons of CDSO and as per Ullage Survey the quantity found at the Port of Chittagong was 17,049.570 metric tons and thus there was difference of only 100.43 metric tons, which was much less than 1%, the permissible limit and this shortage do not attract the aforesaid provisions of the Customs Act. The learned Advocate submitted that the claimed shortage quantity of 236.709 metric tons has been calculated on the basis of the survey made on dip tank reading at shore, which is not permissible under any provisions of law. It has been submitted that the measuring to determine any actual shortage has to be made in the basis of measurement taken on the basis of same type of calculation or method. In the instant case the survey has been made as per Ullage method both at the port of loading and at the port of unloading, hence the said survey reports have to the taken into consideration for determination of the shortage, if any, of the CDSO carried by the carrier to the port of Chittagong. As per Ullage Survey, conducted at the port of loading, the quantity of CDSO carried for Bangladesh was 17063.520 metric tons and at the port of unloading at Chittagong the quantity was found to be 17,049.570 metric tons and thus, there was shortage of only 13.95 metric tons, which is much below the permissible 1% Ocean allowance. The Ullage survey is conducted on board the ship and such survey is universally accepted for which in the aforementioned provisions of the Customs Act, it has been categorically mentioned that the quantity of shortage, if any, has to be found in the conveyance but the Customs Authority as well as the Appellate Tribunal failed to consider this aspect of the law and accordingly, arrived at a wrong decision. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred to a decision of the High Court Division of this Court in the case of James Finlay PLC vs Member (appeal and revision) and Ex-Officio Additional Secretary and others, passed in writ petition No. 70 of 1986 vide judgment and order dated on 13-6-90, wherein also a shortage claim was made by the customs authority on the basis of shore tank measurement and the same was declared to be without lawful authority in making the Rule absolute, wherein their Lordships have accepted the submission of the learned Advocate that the Ullage survey having not been considered by the Customs Authority, the shortage as clamed and the penalty as imposed were bad in law, inasmuch as for the purpose of determining shortage, the shore tank survey was not contemplated under item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 and 156 held that: 
"In the light of the provision of clause 25(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 and in the light of definition of the 'conveyance' as quoted above it can be said that the shortage, if any, has to be found on board the vessel. Therefore, the Ullage Survey Report on Board the vessel, "Botany Trojan" shall prevail against the shore tank survey report in case of any difference in respect of shortage of cargo between the Ullage Survey Report on board the vessel and the Shore Tank Survey Report and that in case the shortage, if any, found in the Ullage Survey on board the vessel is covered by the 1% admissible Ocean allowance then the earlier will not be responsible for any shortage of crude oil found in the Shore Tank Survey Report which is not covered by 1% admissible Ocean allowance and in such case no penalty can be imposed on the carrier or his agent. The respondents have not applied their mind to this aspect of the case." 
6. We have perused the writ petition, the supplementary affidavit and considered the submission of the learned Advocate. We have also perused the decision referred to by the learned Advocate, with which we are in respectful agreement. 
7. Considering the facts as detailed above and the submissions made by the learned Advocate, we find that issue involved in this Rule is, whether there was any shortage in the delivery of the cargo, which falls within the purview of item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, having regard to the permissible 1% Ocean allowance. 
8. The admitted facts are that the vessel MT Jamac carried cargo for two countries, namely, Bangladesh and Singapore. The cargo for Bangladesh Port was Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) and as per declared manifest the cargo quantity carried for Bangladesh was 17,150 metric tons, whereas as per Ullage Survey conducted at the port of loading the quantity measured was 17,063.52 metric tons and that as per Ullage Survey conducted at the port of delivery, that is, at Chittagong Port the quantity was measured at 17,049.570 metric tons and that as per dip reading shore tank measurement the quantity delivered was measured at 16,913.291 metric tons. The learned Advocate submitted that Ullage Survey is a method by which the measurement of the liquid cargo carried by a vessel is taken on board the vessel, which is universally accepted. Thus, as per Ullage Survey the quantity of cargo carried for Bangladesh was 17,063.526 metric tons and the cargo carried to the port of Chittagong was found to be 17,049.57 metric tons and thus there was actually a shortage of only 13.95 metric tons, which is negligibly less than the permissible limit of 1% allowed as Ocean allowance. It further appears that the difference, between the declared manifest quantity of 17,150 metric tons and the Ullage Survey Report quantity of 17,049.570 metric tons, found at Chittagong comes to 100.43 metric tons, which is also within the permissible limit of 1% allowance as Ocean allowance. The difference between the declared manifest quantity and the dip reading shore tank measurement quantity shows a shortage of 236.709 metric tons. The learned Advocate referring to the provisions of item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) submitted that such shortage on the basis of shore tank reading is not contemplated by section 156 of the Customs Act and that section 156 of the Customs Act contemplates that measurement must be taken on the conveyance, that is, on board the vessel. In order to appreciate the said submission of the learned Advocate the relevant provision of law i.e. item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1), is reproduced below: 
"156. Punishment for offences : (1) Whoever commits an offence described in column-1 of the table below shall in addition to and not in derogation of any punishment to which he may be liable under any other law, be liable to the punishment mentioned against that offence in column 2 thereof: 

Table

Offence (1)

Penalties (2)

Section (3)

24. (i) If any goods entered in the import manifest of a conveyance are not found in that conveyance; or

 

(ii) If the quantity found in the conveyance is short, and the shortage is not accounted for to the satisfaction of the Officer-in-Charge of the Customs house. (Underlining is ours)

 

The persons-in-charge of such conveyance shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding twice the amount of duty chargeable on the goods not found on the conveyance or, if such goods are not dutiable or the duty thereon cannot be ascertained, to a penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand Taka for every missing or deficient package or separate article and in the case of bulk-goods to a penalty not exceeding the value of the goods, or fifty thousand Taka whichever be higher."

 

45, 53 & 55

 
9. On plain reading of the aforesaid provision of item No. 24(ii) we do not find any ambiguity in the law in accepting the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner inasmuch as it has been clearly mentioned that "If the quantity found in the conveyance is short", which means the measurement has to be taken on board the vessel which carried the cargo. It further appears from the materials on record that for carrying the cargo (CDSO), the vessel is allowed 1% in the difference of measurement as to the quantity carried, as Ocean allowance. Now considering the difference between quantity carried (17,063.52 mt) and delivered (17,049.57 mt) both as per the Ullage Survey Report i.e. survey conducted, at the port of loading and at the port of delivery respectively, which was calculated at (17,063.52 mt-17,049.57 mt) 13.95 of metric tons and which is much less than the permissible limit of 1% and the difference between the declared manifest quantity (17,150 mt) and the Ullage Survey Report quantity (17049.57) at the port of delivery was 100.40 metric tons, which is also less than 1% compared to the quantity of CDSO carried by the vessel for Chittagong. Thus we do not find any such shortage for which the vessel can be held responsible for an offence as contemplated under item 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act. The measurement of the shore tank has no relevance in the instant case. We get support from the decision to which the learned Advocate referred to being the judgment and order dated 13-6-90 passed in Writ Petition No. 70/1986, wherein their Lordships in making the Rule absolute have held that in item 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 the words "quantity found in the conveyance" means the quantity found as per measuring taken on board the ship as per Ullage Survey method. Therefore, the Ullage Survey Report on board the vessel prevails against the Shore Tank Survey Report. The question of shortage as contemplated by item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, the 1% admissible Ocean allowance on the quantity carried by the vessel must be taken into consideration, and therefore, the vessel/carrier cannot be held responsible for any shortage below 1% and such shortage cannot be said to be an offence committed under item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969. 
10. On perusal of the impugned order it appears that the Tribunal has taken notice of the report of the Ullage Survey conducted both at the port of loading and at the port of delivery but the Tribunal due to non-application of mind as to the provision of item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act failed to consider that the shortage, if any, has to be calculated on the basis of the measurements taken on board the vessel taken as per Ullage Survey conducted both at the port of loading and at the pod of delivery and such a shortage cannot be calculated on the basis of survey conducted at the shore tanks as has been held by their Lordships in the judgment and order dated 13-6-90 passed in Writ Petition No. 70 of 1986 as mentioned earlier. Thus we find merit in the Rule. 
Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 5-3-98 passed by the Customs Excise & VAT Appellate Tribunal in disposing of the appeal arising out of Order No. 87/97 dated 29-4-97 passed by the Commissioner of Customs Excise and VAT (Appeal) affirming the appeal, evidenced by Annexure-L to the writ petition, is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The shortage of CDSO as found in this case does not attract the provision of item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act and thus the vessel did not commit any offence thereunder. 
End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney General, instructed by Mr. B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners (In both the cases) 
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondents (In both the cases)
parties:
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Petitioners (In both the cases)
Vs.
Md. Masud Miah ------ Respondent (In both the cases)
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25.2.2010 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.1784 and 1785 of 2009)
full_judgment:
S.K. Sinha J. These petitions arise out of the same case and therefore, these petitions are disposed of analogously by this order.

2. While the respondent Md. Masud Miah was working as Superintendent of Police, CID, Dhaka, he had faced departmental proceeding containing twelve counts of charge on 25th April, 2005. An inquiry officer was appointed to inquire into the allegations, who found five counts proved and recommended taking legal action against him. He was ultimately removed from the service by order dated 31st January, 2006. He, thereupon, moved the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka a petition The Lawyers under section 4(1) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 against the said order of removal. The Administrative Tribunal by judgment and order dated 13th June, 2007 allowed the petition in part, maintained his punishment made under section 3(a) and 3(d) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 but converted his punishment to one under section 4(3) (a) of the said Rules and demoted him to the rank of Additional Superintendent of Police for a period of 5(five) years with effect from 31st January, 2006.

3. Respondent being aggrieved by the said order of demotion preferred Administrative Appellate Tribunal Appeal No.169 of 2007. The petitioners also preferred Administrative Appellate Tribunal Appeal No. 219 of 2007 against the same judgment before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal heard both the appeals separately and disposed of them by two separate judgments on 24th June 2009, allowing Appeal No. 169 of 2007 by setting aside the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal and dismissing the other Appeal No. 219 of 2007.

4. The petitioners thereupon moved this Division in Civil Petition Nos.1784 and 1785 of 2009. This Division dismissed both the petitions by two separate judgments on 25th February, 2010. The petitioners thereupon moved these petitions.

<u>5. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General appearing for the petitioners, has taken us to the judgments and argued that since the appeals had arisen out or the same judgment, it was incumbent upon the Administrative Appellate Tribunal to hear and dispose of both the appeals analogously   in order to avoid conflicting decisions, and as a matter of fact, it had delivered two conflicting judgments, which escaped the notice of this Division while disposing of the leave petitions and the same is an error of law apparent on the face of the record. It is further contended that the Administrative Tribunal while maintaining the punishment of the respondent came to a definite finding that some of the charges brought against the respondent had been satisfactorily proved but the Administrative Appellate Tribunal without reversing those findings allowed the appeal preferred by the respondent   mechanically. In view of the above, it is contended that the judgments of this Division deserve reconsideration for ends of justice.</u>

6. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud entering caveat submitted that the inconsistency cropped up in the judgments had been corrected by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal by order dated 27th August, 2009 in Administrative Appellate Tribunal Appeal Nos. 219 and 169 of 2007. Learned counsel submitted that the points raised in the review petitions had already been addressed by this Division and therefore, these review petitions are not legally maintainable.

<u>7. We have perused the judgments and heard the learned counsel at the Bar. The Administrative Tribunal upon consideration of the materials on record observed that the enquiry officer on proper appreciation of the materials on record rightly found the charge in respect of count Nos.1, 7 and 9 proved against the respondent. The Appellate Tribunal while allowing Appeal No.169 of 2007 observed "we do not find any cause and material on record to hold the petitioner guilty to the charge. So far as other charges are concerned the inquiry officer himself concluded that this could not be successfully proved in the facts and circumstances the case and the materials on record. We are constrained to hold that the charges against the petitioner could not be proved by any cogent and dependable evidence and as such the impugned punishment being essentially passed on 31st January, 2006 cannot sustainable in law". While dismissing the other appeal, the Appellate Tribunal observed that "we are satisfied that the learned Tribunal (illg) carefully considered all material facts at issue and decided these with reference to the materials on record. The findings arrived at by the learned Tribunal arc supported by reasons. We do not find any illegality or material irregularity in the impugned judgment which may justify any interference by us in appeal. In fact, the impugned judgment is well written and well-reasoned which is amply supported by materials on record".</u>

8. There is no gainsaying fact that the Appellate Tribunal made inconsistent findings which had escaped the notice of this Division. Though the Administrative Appellate Tribunal corrected the judgments on 27th August, 2009 on the reasoning’s that the copying clerk made the mistake in typing the operating portion of the judgment in Appeal No.219 of 2007, the Appellate Tribunal did not make correction in respect of the inconsistent findings and reasoning’s in the judgments. There is, therefore apparent errors in the judgments. In view of the above, we find merit in these petitions. Leave is, therefore, granted in both the cases to consider the additional grounds as under:

"I. Because the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal having been challenged in two appeals, one by the respondent another by the Government, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed error in not disposing of two appeals by one judgment and this Court committed an error apparent on the face of the record in not noticing the said wrong committed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal.

II. Because the Administrative Tribunal having found the respondent guilty, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal most illegally set aside the said judgment in the appeal filed by the respondent, whereas affirmed the said judgment in the appeal filed by the Government and this Court committed error on the face of the record in affirming such contradictory judgments passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal.

III. Because the Administrative Tribunal having found the allegation Nos. 1, 3, 7 and 9 of the enquiry report as correct and having found the respondent guilty, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal most illegally allowed the appeal No. 169 of 2007 filed by the respondent without reversing the aforesaid finding of the Administrative Tribunal and this Court committed an error apparent on the face of the record in affirming the said judgment in Civil Petition Nos. 1784 and 1785 of 2009, thus the judgment passed in the said civil Petition is required to be reviewed.

9. Petitioners are permitted to prepare the paper book out of Court in accordance No. 1037 of 2008 with rules.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney General, Instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellant
Mahmudul Islam and Probir Neogi, Senior Advocates, Instructed by Nurul Islam Chowdhury, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondents
parties:
Government of Bangladesh ------ Appellant
Vs.
Mr. Khoshal and others ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 25.05.2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 389 of 2001)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain, J. This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 25.06.2009 passed by High Court Division in First Appeal No. 389 of 2001 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 25.06.2009 passed by the then learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Gazipur, Dismissing the suit. The facts, leading to the filing of this appeal, in a nutshell, are;

2. On 05.08.1993, the plaintiff, the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Gazipur, instituted Title Suit No. 107 of 1994 in the Second Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Gazipur against the defendants for declaration of title over the two suit ponds measuring about 19.35 acres. The Plaintiffs case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to the then Emperor of India. Two tanks situated in the suit land are being used by local people. At the time of S.A. operation, the said two tanks were recorded as Khas land in the name of erstwhile East Pakistan. But at the time of R.S. operation, the defendants recorded the land measuring about 12.12 acres in their names. Such recording was wrong and imaginary. It was also the case of the plaintiff that the suit tanks has been in the possession of the plaintiff-Government for more than 70 years. The Government has allowed local people to use both the tanks for their welfare. But the defendants have been trying to prevent the local people from using the two tanks on the strength of wrong ROR, which is to be corrected. Hence the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit for declaration of title over the two suit tanks measuring about 19.35 acres.

3. The defendants-respondents contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material statements made in the plaint. Their case, in short, is the suit filed by the plaintiff is not maintainable in its present form and that it is barred by limitation. Their further case is that defendant predecessor late Daliludding Ahmed, a high official of British era obtained permanent lease of the suit land from the then Sreephaltali Estate and had been paying rent. During S A record, said land measuring about 19.35 acres was properly and correctly recorded in the name of Daliluddin Ahmed. Later, in 1990 some interested people by making application to the land Reform Board tried to declare the suit land as khas. On such application, an enquiry was held and according to the enquiry reports, submitted by the officers at the field and on the basis of ROR the evil design failed and the property was properly recorded in the names of the defendants. The defendants have since been possessing the land by growing jackfruit trees, mango trees etc. and also fishing in the tanks and by paying rent up to 1994. The Plaintiff never took any step for correction of record in any manner till the filing of the suit.

4. The trial Court upon hearing the parties by its judgment and order dated 29.1.2000 dismissed the suit.

5. Being aggrieved by the Judgment and decree passed by the trial court, the plaintiff-Government preferred First Appeal No. 389 of 2001 before the High Court Division. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties by the judgment and order dated 25.06.2009 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court.

6. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiff-Appellant filed Civil petition for leave to Appeal No. 35 of 2010 in which, leave was granted on 15.05.2011, resulting in Civil appeal No. 171 of 2011.

7. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General, appearing for the appellant, submits that the Government has filed the suit claiming title to the suit plot No. 56 will an area 7.97 acres and plot No. 62 with an area of 11.30 acres as tanks and that the water of those tanks is being used by the local people for meeting their daily requirement and that the High Court Division without deciding the question of possession of its perspective discharged the Rule and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside. He further submits that the plaintiff-respondents miserably failed to prove their title to and possession in the suit land and that the High Court Division without looking into these aspects discharged the Rule and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside.

8. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, supports the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division. No further submits that plaintiff miserably failed to prove its title to and possession in the two disputed tanks and as such, no interference is called for.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Attorney General and learned Senior Advocate, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

10. Before entering into the merit of the appeal, it is necessary to go through the grounds, on which, Leave was granted. The grounds are quoted below:

"I. Because the High Court Division having found that the suit land belonged to the Emperor of India appearing in the first part of the judgment but its subsequent finding in the later part of the judgment that the same belonged to Zaminder is an apparent mistake on the face of record and falsity or otherwise of the entire story of settlement from the Zaminder, as claimed by the defendants, was considered by the High Court Division in its proper perspective.

II. Because the trial court and the High Court Division have failed to consider that before acquisition of rent-receiving interest there cannot be any cause of action to file an application under section 19(2) of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that the rent receiving interest of Dhaka where the suit plot at the relevant time was situated having been acquired in the year 1963, the alleged case under section 53 of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act is collusive and void and without considering the aforesaid legal provisions and the courts below erred in law in relying upon the Judgment of special appeal No. 239 of 1962 in finding title in favour of the defendant-respondent.

III. Because the Government have filed the suit claiming the suit plot No. 56 with an area of 7.97 acres and plot No. 62 with an area 11.30 acres as ponds and its water is being used by the local people for meeting their daily requirement and in deciding he instant suit and the courts below considered the aforesaid claims of the Government in its proper perspective, ignoring the public utility."

<u>11. Admittedly, the suit tanks originally belonged to the emperor of India as the superior landlord. There are two tanks in the suit land, during B.A. operation, the two tanks were recorded in the name of the then Government of East Pakistan in Khash Khatian No. 1, but during R.S. operation those two tanks measuring an area of about 12.12 acres were recorded in the names the defendants. It is the consistent case of the plaintiff that the villagers had been possessing and using both the suit tanks for their own welfare for the last 70 years. The plaintiff also claimed that the defendants started creating obstacle to the local people in possessing the using the suit tanks.</u>

<u>12. Having gone through the Judgment of the Courts below including the High Court Division, we find that much importance was given to the judgment passed in the special Appeal No. 239 of 1962 under section 53 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Let us now consider about the said judgment. Admittedly the PRR was recorded in the name of the ex-landlord in respect of Plot Nos. 56 and 62 of Khatian No. 1/27 of Mouza-Dakurail, Police Station Kaliakoir. Against the said entry made in the PRR, Daliluddin Ahmed filed objection case No. 3053 for recording the land in his name alleging that he had taken pattan of those two tanks from the landlord. The objection case was allowed by the objection officer. Against that order of objection officer, or the Government, one Amiruddin filed an Appeal No. 1614 under section 19(2) of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act on behalf of the villagers of Dakurail and Dhol Samudra Kutamani. The appellate officer allowed the appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but ordered that those two tanks be recorded "in the name of the Government with note in remark column-23 that those tanks would be useable by the public. After that, Daliluddn Ahmmed filed Special appeal No. 239 of 1962 under section 53 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Special Judge allowed the appeal on technical ground that neither the Government nor outgoing landlord filed any appeal under Section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act. But one third - person namely, Amiruddin on behalf of the villagers filed appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, the learned Special Judge held that the appeal filed under Section 19(2) of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act by Amiruddin on behalf of the villagers was incompetent. As such, the learned special Judge allowed the appeal under section 53 of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act filed by Daliluddin Ahmmed and the judgment and order passed in Appeal No. 1615 under Section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was set aside as not maintainable and restored the order of objection officer who recorded the Khatian in the name of Daliluddin Ahmmed.</u>

13. On consideration of the judgment delivered in Special Appeal No. 239 of 1962, we find that appeal No. 1615 under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and tenancy act was filed by one Amiruddin on behalf of the villagers. In the judgment of Appeal No. 239 of 1962 nothing was stated whether the said Amiruddin who filed Appeal No. 1615 under section 19(2) of the state Acquisition and Tenancy Act was heard or not. In the Judgment delivered in the special case nothing was stated about the claim of title by Daliluddin Ahmmed. Only on technical ground the special Appeal No. 239 of 1962 was allowed. Though the villagers of two villages were the most aggrieved persons, they were not heard at all.

14. On consideration of the evidence of D.W. 1, Rafiqul Islam Bakshi, we find that he deposed on behalf of the defendants as their attorney. The examination and cross examination of D.W. 1 was completed on 26.05.1998. Subsequently, on recall he again deposed before the Court on 16.07.2000. On that date, during examination in Chief, he filed three original copies of pattannama of 1352 B.S. marked as exhibit-Jha series covering an area of 19.35 acres of land. While exhibiting those documents, this witness did not state anything why those documents could not be filed on 26.05.1998 when this witness was examined and cross-examined. This aspect of the case has also not been considered by any of the courts below.

15. As regards possession, all the courts below found possession of the defendants in the suit land because of preparation of Khatian in their names and also for payment of rent by them. The Government only examined one witness, P.W. 1 namely. Wali Ahmed, Tahsildar of Fathepur Union Land office but none of the villagers was examined although the plaintiff filed the suit on the assertion that the villagers of two villages have been possessing and using the disputed two tanks for their welfare for the last 70 years, Even on behalf of the villagers one Amiruddin filed Appeal No. 1615 under 19(2) of the State acquisition and Tenancy Act and accordingly, the khatian was prepared in the name of the Government in khash Khatian No. 1 with a noting in remark column -23 that those tanks would be useable by the public, The judgment delivered in Appeal No. 1615, was, however, set aside in Special Appeal No. 239 of 1962.

<u>16. Having considered all the aspects of the case, we are of the view that the determination of possession of both the suit tanks was of prime importance in the present case and the question of possession has not been resolved properly by any of the courts below. Therefore, we are inclined to send the case on remand to the trial court for affording the plaintiffs (Government) to examine witnesses from two villages as the villagers are alleged to have been in possession of both the suit tanks. The defendants will also be at liberty to examine witnesses if they so desire.</u>

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and the judgment and decree of the trial Court are set aside and the suit is remanded to the trial court for disposing of it in accordance with the direction given in the body of the judgment. There is no order as to costs.

End.
