Niranjan Prasad Barua being dead his heirs : Promotosh Barua and Ors ----- Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J :- This Rule arises out of an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the judgment and decree dated 9.4.1990 (decree signed on 16.4.1990) passed in other Appeal No. 77 of 1986 by the District Judge, Chittagong affirming, those passed by the then Munsif, First Court, Patiya, Chittagong in other Suit No. 298 of 1983.
 2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed other suit No. 100 of 1975 in the court of the 4th court of Munsif at Patia, Chittagong for declaration that the suit property is benami one and that it be declared that the defendant No. 1 since deceased has got no right, title and inter-est in the suit land. The case was subsequently transferred to the First Court of Munsif at Patia. Chittagong and it was renumbered as other Suit no. 298 of 1983. 

3. Facts of the case, in short, are that the schedule land belonged to Rajapur Barue of Pancharia, Upazila Patia, District Chittagong. The landlord of the schedule land instituted Rent Suit No. 782 of 1945 and got decree and in Rent Execution case No. 402 of 1945 he got bainama and was let into possession. The disputed land is within compact area of plaintiffs dwelling house where is a tank and pucca ghat and on the bank of the tank there are many fruit bearing trees. The plaintiff being seared of money lender and the landlord in particular who is very much inimical to the plaintiff he purchased the same in the name of defendant No. 1 since deceased who was nephew of the plaintiff and whose house is located three miles off from the disputed tank. The principle defendant No. 1 has got no right title and interest in the suit land and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is in possession of the suit by' paying government revenue and for long use of the land the plaintiff has acquired perfect title by adverse possession. The defendant No. I also wanted to executed a deed of relinquishment but the plaintiff was unmindful. The bainama and writ of delivery of possession are lying with the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and S. A. Khatian and B. S. Khatian also stands correctly recorded in the name of the plaintiff opposite party No. I. The defendant No. 2 took loan of Taka 500/- from the plaintiff opposite party and on repeated demand the defendant No. 1 is not in the loan amount and this has embittered relationship with the defendant No. 1 and-as such the defendant No. 1 threatened to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land and the plaintiff opposite party who is a poor teacher cannot withstand the onslaught of the defendant No. I who is very much powerful with man and money and who has got no regard for law of the land and as such the plaintiff prayed for injunction restraining the defendant No. I from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiff till disposal of the suit. in the original plaint there was a prayed for directing the defendant No. 1 to execute the kabala which has been subsequently deleted at the prayed of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 by amendment of the plaint vide order dated 11-1-87. 

4. The defendant No. 1 since dead entered appearance and filed written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaintiff and contending, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable. The defendant No. 1 categorically denied that he is benamder of the plaintiff and con-tended that he purchased the disputed land by his hard earned money. He further stated that he placed possession of the suit land in the hands of added defendants who are his nephews and they are possessing the disputed tank on his behalf. He also denied that S. A. and B. S. Khatian stands recorded in the name of the plaintiff or that any right, title or inter-est is created in his favour and as such he prayed for dismissal of the suit. 
5. During pendency of the suit the defendant No. 1 died and his heirs were duly substituted but ultimately they did not contest the suit. 

6. The petitioner of this revisional application were added as defendant No. 4-8 in the original suit at their instance and filed written statements in the suit denying the material allegations of the plaintiff and contending, interalia that the suit land was purchased by their predecessor-in-interest late Nagendra Lai Barua, who used to serve at Assam, by his hard earned money. Late Nagendra Lal Barua got the land purchased is the benami of his near relative, defendant No. 1 and late Nagendra Lal Barua since deceased used to possess the disputed land and after his death his heirs the added defendant petitioners are in possession of the suit land by paying government revenue and P. S. and B. S. Khatian stands in the name of Lice defendant petitioners. They are possessing the suit land and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 have no right, title and interest in the suit land. 

7. The learned Munsif, First Court Patia, Chittagong ultimately tried the suit and after considering the materials and evidence on record decreed the suit and against, the said judgment and decree of the trial court these defendant petitioners preferred other Appeal No. 77 of 1986 before the court of learned District Judge, Chittagong and the learned District Judge, Chittagong judgment and decree dated 9-4-1990 dismissed the appeal by affirming the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif, Patia. Chittagong and against the said judgment and decree dated 9-4-1990 of the learned District Judge, Chittagong the defendant petitioners moved this court and obtained the pre-sent Rule. 

8. Mr. Abdul Momin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioners mainly argues on 3 (three) points-namely, that the elements of benami transaction are missing in the suit„ that the suit is hit by section 66 sub-section (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the suit is not properly valued. 

9. On the other hand, Mr. Nikhiles Datta, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff apposite party No. 1 submits that although the courts below did not elaborately discussed the elements of benami transaction but nevertheless it appears from a plain reading of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial court that both the courts below had considered the elements of the benami transaction and after taking into consideration the elements of benami transaction along with the facts and circumstances of the case both the courts below decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff opposite party NO. 1 has been able to prove the case by cogent and sufficient. Mr. Datta next submits that it appears from a perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial court that both the courts below took into consideration the objection raised by the defendant petitioners as to maintain-ability of the suit in the light of the provisions as laid down in section 66 of sub-section (1) of the code of Civil Procedure and both the courts below rightly and legally arrived at a concurrent finding that the instant suit is not hit by section 66 sub-section (1) of the said Code in as much as the principle contesting the suit not anybody claiming under him is resisting the claim of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and in that view of the matter the suit is not hit by section 66 (1) of the code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate further submits that it is a suit for declaration simpliciter for declaring that the defendant No. 1 is the benamder of the plaintiff and since the plaintiff is in possession, the plaintiff has filed the suit with fixed court fee and since it is a suit for simple declaration there is no objective standard to determine the valuation of the suit and as such the plaintiff rightly valued the suit at Taka 14/which was the value of the auction purchase of the suit land. 

10. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears to me that the learned appellate court below found that the principle defendant No. 1 (since dead) was the benamder of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and the appellate court-below also found that since purchase of the suit land in the benami of the principal defendant No. 1 the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is in possession of the suit land and the appellate court below also found that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 purchased the suit land with his own money and for his own benefit in the benami of principal defendant No. 1. The appellate court below also found that the suit is not hit or barred under section 66(1) of the Code of Civil procedure inasmuch as the principal defendant No. 1 or his heirs did not ultimately contest the suit. The appellate court below taking into consideration all the materials and evidence on record found that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been able to prove his case that the principal defendant No. 1 was his benamder and he purchased the suit land with his own money for his own benefit and he was all through in possession of the suit land since auction purchase through the principal defendant No. 1 and he also proved by sufficient materials that the defendant No. 1 was his benamder and, thus, it appears that the learned appellate court below concurred with the finding of the trial court with regard to the possession of the suit land by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and that the suit is not barred by section 66(1) of the code of Civil procedure and that the principal , defendant No. 1 was a benamder of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 got the suit land with his own money and for his own benefit. 

11. Now let us take the second sub-mission of Mr. Chowdhury first J. e. that the suit is not maintainable under section 66(1) Of the Code of Civil procedure. During the cause of argument on this point Mr. Chowdhury referred to the following decisions : namely 1. L. R. 21(A11) 238,'--A. I. R 1982 (Andhraprodesh) 49, A. I. R. 1951 (Mad) 943 A. I. R 1964 (SC) 1124 and relying on these decisions he argued that if the plaintiff make a statement in the plaint. that the defendant No. 1 is the benamder of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 is a certified purchaser in that case the suit is hit by section 66(1) of the code and the suit is liable to be dismissed as barred under section 66(1) of the Code Section 66(1) of the code came up for consideration before different High Courts of this Sub-continent including this division. Before we take up the point let us quote section itself which reads as follows : "66(1) No. suit shall be maintained against any person claiming title under a purchase certified by the Court in such 
manner as may be prescribed on the ground that the purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff or on behalf of some one through whom the plaintiff claims." This section corresponds to original section 317 of the code. Section 317 came up for consideration before the Allahabad 
High Court. In the case of Kishen Lal Vs. Garuruddhways Prashad and others the Allahabad High Court observed. The opening words no suit shall be maintained mean, we have no doubt, "no suit shall be instituted, and if such a suit be instituted it shall fail," That is the only meaning we can attach to the word "mentioned". Their  lordship further observed. The object of 
the section was no doubt to prevent judgment debtors from purchasing their own property at auction in the name of another and for that purpose the section provided that no suit shall lie against the certified purchaser on the ground that the purchase was benami. The section does not 
designate any particular person or class of persons as being the person who shall not sue. It confines itself to indicating the person who shall not be impleaded as defendant in a suit instituted on the specific ground mentioned. In that way it prevent judgment debtors who have purchased in the names of others persons from suits the certified purchasers for possession that is to say, it permits the benami curtailed purchaser to reap the benefit of his fraud by barring the real purchaser from suing him, and if it also prevents the creditors of such a judgment debtors from suing the certified purchaser, it may will be that that evil is not unequally balanced in that case their Lordship were of the opinion that the suit was barred under section 317 of the code which corresponds to section 66(1) of the present code. In that case the certified purchaser was in possession and he resisted the claim of the plaintiff. But in the instant case the plaintiff is found to be possession of the property and the benamder did not contest the suit. So, the facts, of the instant case are quite distinguishable from the fact of that case and the decision has no manner of 
application in the instant case. 

12. The next case is A. i. R. 1962 (Andhra Prodesh) 49 wherein it has been held that section 66 is based on public policy, the primary object being that the certified purchase should be conclusive and to prevent its being challenged. The purpose of that section is obviously to 
check the practice of judgment debtors making secret purchase in the names of their relations or friends at court auctions. It is with this aim that the embargo was laid on a suit found on the pleaa of benami. This does not render benami sales illegal or invalid but it only places a procedure bar to the enforceability of a claim that the plaintiff is the real owner and the auction purchaser was only benamder. In that suit their lordship opined that any suit founded upon the Averments that the auction purchase was not intended to benefit the purchaser he being only benamder but the beneficial owner was the plaintiff, falls within the range of section 66 C. P. C. irrespective of the fact that the certified purchaser happened to be the agent of the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In that case theirs of the certified purchaser contested the suit so the provision of section 66(1) of the code was attracted and the case reported in 27 C. W. No. 208 was also not considered. In A. I. R. 1951 (mad) 943, the similar principal has been laid down that section 66 lays down an embargo on the plea of benami when it forms the basis of a suit by the person claiming to be the real owner against a court auction purchaser alleged to be a benamder As the section places a procedural bar to the enforceability of a claim based on benami which is otherwise quite legal and valid and effective the section has to be strictly construed. Their lordship further observed that but when substantially the facts attract the operation of the rule enacted by the Section, court will be failing in their duty if effect is not given to it. The facts of this case are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case algid as such it has no manner of application in the instant case. In A. 1. R. 1964 (SC) 1254 the Indian supreme court in interpreting section 66 and order 6 rule 2 of the code observed that protection under sub section (1) of section 66 is available against real purchaser and per-sons claiming through him. The plaintiffs claim is based upon the benami nature of the transaction and that cannot stand because of section 66 of the code of civil procedure bars it. The facts of this case are also distinguishable in that the person claiming through the certified purchaser resisted the claim of the plaintiff and the case reported in 27 C. W. N. 208 and A. 1. R 1925 (All) 47 were neither referred to no considered by the supreme court. In A. I. R. 1967 (SC) 1124, the Indian supreme court held that transactions which are called benami are lawful and are prohibit-ed. When it is alleged that a person in whose name the property is purchased or entered in the public record is not the real owner, the court may, if the claim is proved, grant relief upholding the claim of the real owner, But section 66(1) seeks to oust the jurisdiction of the court to give effect to real as against benami title. The object of the clause is to prevent claims before the civil court that the certified purchaser purchased the property benami for another person. Thereby the jurisdiction of the civil court to give effect to the real as against the nominal title is restricted and the section must be strictly construed. Where a person alleges that a property purchased at a court auction was purchased on his behalf or on behalf of some one through whom he claims, the suit is clearly barred. But where the claim is that the properties belonged to the joint family because they were purchased with the aid of joint family bound in the name of the benamder such a claim does not fall with-in the terms of section 66(1) of the code. This decision also in fact, does not help Mr. Chowdhury in as much as the facts the facts are quite distinguishable. As against that Mr. Nikhiles Datta, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, relies on the case reported in 27 C. W. N. 208, which is also published in A. 1. R. 1923 (Calcutta) 302 and also 4.6.3, Indian Cases Volume 75 at page 96. In 27 C. W. N. case it has been held that section 66 of the code of civil procedure has no application in a case where the benamder himself did not claim under the sale certificate. In that case the benamder did not appear or resist the claim of the real owner. In that view of the matter their lordship held that section 66(1) has no manner of application when the certified purchaser or his successor does not con-test the claim of the real owner. In A. I. R--1925 (All) 47 the Alahabad High Court held that section 66 of the code of civil procedure is not a bar when the certified purchaser does not contest plaintiffs claim. Section 66 of the code of Civil procedure only applies when the plaintiff attempts to assert title as against the certified purchaser but what the certified purchaser does not contest the plaintiffs claim the suit is not barred. The case reported in A. 1. R. 1936 (All) 750 namely, the case of Most. Asghari Begum and another Vs. Kanhasiya Lal and others was a suit for declaration that the plaintiff are true owners of the property on the ground that auction purchase was benami for them. The sons of auction purchaser did not come forward to contest their claim. It was held that section 66 was no bar to the suit as the section provided for a suit only against a certified purchaser or persons claiming under him. It did not exclude evidence as to auction purchase being Benami when such evidence was relevant for the purpose of determining title between plaintiff and a third person. 

13. On a perusal of all these decisions it appears that the cases relied on by Mr. Chowdhury do not help him in that the facts of those cases distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In these cases the benamder himself resisted the claim of the plaintiff and in those cases, the case reported in 27 C. W. N. 208-A. I. R. 1923 Cal. 302, A. 1.R. 1925 (All) 47 and the case reported in A. I. R. 1936(A11) 750 were neither referred to nor considered. I think that the decisions belied on by Mr. Datta are relevant for determine the most question in the instant case because in those cases the fight was between real owner and the third party. and all the courts of this subcontinent is of consensus opinion that when the real owner sues a defendant claiming that the defendant is his benamder, the suit will be hit by section 66(1) of the Code of Civil procedure if the claim of the real owner is resisted by the benamder himself or any persons claiming title through him. The cases referred to and relied by Mr. Chowdhury show that these were cases in which the claim of the real owner was resisted their by the benamder himself or some one claiming through him. in some other eases the opinion passed by their lordships are practically obiter dictum and not ratio decidendi inasmuch as in some of the cases namely the case reported in A. 1. R. 1957 (SC) 1124, is not a suit against benamder and the observations made by their lordships are practically biter dictum. In the case of Sri Sri Kishore Benwari Jugme Bigrahadi Paramesh Jawa Vs. Ajit Kumar Nandi and other reported in A. I. R 1938 (Cal) 874, their lordships considered the case reported in 27 C. W. N. 208 and observed that where the certified purchaser does not contest, on question of bar under section 66 Arises. The case reported in 27' C. W. N. 208 was approvingly quoted in the case of Roi Bohadur Barajonder Mohan Mitra and others Vs. Tamil Uddin Bisas and others reported in 16 D. L. R 125. In that case it has been held that "in the case reported in 27 C. W. N. it has been held that section 66 of the code has no application in a case where the Banamder himself does not claim under the sale certificate." It was further held in that case that the object of section 66 of Code is to give protection to the benamder and thus to discharge benami purchasers. It was never the intention of the legislature to give any protection to a party interested in the benami purchase. It was also held in that case that provisions of section 66 being contrary to quotable principal must be construed strictly any should never be extended beyond its legitimate limits. Similarly in another case reported in 22. D. L. R. 858, it has been held that when the plaintiff sues against the benamder then only bar would operate but no otherwise. 

14. There is another line of decision on the interpretation of section 66 of the code of civil procedure. In the case reported in Indian cases volume 25 at page 810, it has been held that a real purchaser when in uninterrupted possession of the suit land can maintain a suit against the benamder to defend his possession and the suit would not be barred under section 66 of the code of civil procedure. The sin similar view has been in the case reported In A. I. R. 1935 (All) 143. From a view of all these decisions it is crystal clear that the superior courts of this subcontinent ale of consensus opinion that it a real owner hearings an action against the certified purchaser to assert his title and the certified purchaser himself or any body claiming under him resists the claim of the real owner then the suit is hit by section 66(1) real owner against the certificate purchaser and certificate purchaser or any body claiming under him does not contest or resist the claim of the real owner then section 66(1) of the code bus no manner of application. It further appears that the cases relied on by Mr. Datta namely the case reported in 27 C. W. N. 208 A. I. R 1925 (111) 47 and A. I. R. 1936 (All) 750 were not referred to or discussed in the cases relied on by Mr. Chowdhury. It appears that these three cases relied on by Mr. Datta where not cited in those cases. Moreover the facts of those 3 (three) cases are similar to the facts of the present case in that in cases the claim of the real owner was not resisted by the alleged benamder or some one claiming through him. In the instant case we find that though at the initial stage the principal defendant No. 1 who was the alleged benamder entered his appearance and filed written statement denying the claim of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 but he died during tendency of the suit and heirs were substituted in due course but ultimately the heirs of principal defendant No. 1 did not contest the suit rather it is the added defendants namely defendant Nos. 408 who ultimately contested the suit. The fact of this case are exactly similar to the fact of the case reported in A. I. R. 1936 (All) 750. 

14.(a) On a perusal of all the decisions as referred by the learned Advocate of both the sides it appears to me that then consensus opinion of the superior course of this subcontined with regard to interpretation of section 66(1) of the code civil procedure is that when a suit is instituted by the real owner claiming his title against the benamder and the benamder comes forward and resist the claim of the real owner the matter ends there and the suit is hit by section 66(1) of the code. But where the real owner instituted a suit against the benamder claiming that benamder is not the real owner simply benamder and if the benamder or any one claiming under him does not come for-warded to contest the claim of the plaintiff in that case section 66(1) of the said code will having manner of application and the suit would not be barred under the said provisions of the code and this seems to be consistent view of the Calcutta High Court and Allahabad High Court the Indian Jurisdiction and the case reported in 27 C. W. N. 208 has been approvingly quoted by this Division in the case reported in 16  D. L. R 125 at paragraph 10. In view of my aforesaid discussions I think that the sub-missions made by Mr. Chowdhury would have force had the benamder or his heirs ultimately contested the suit. Since the benamder or his heirs did not contest the suit I find that the suit is not hit by section 66(1) of the code of civil procedure and for that purpose I rely on the decisions referred to above by Mr. Datta. 

15. Next submission of Chowdhury is that in decreeing the suit both the courts below failed to consider the elements of the benami transaction. He submitted that in a case where it is alleged that the defendant was the benamder of the plaintiff the court must consider those elements namely the source of money, possession of the property, custody of the documents and facts and circumstances of the case. Mr. Chowdhury submits that the instant case if we scrutinize the impugned judgment as well as the judgment for the trial court we find that both the courts below failed to approach the matter from that angle. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the appellate court below did not spell out in so many words what are the elements of benami transaction but it decreeing the suit both the courts below concurrently found that the two vital documents namely the sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession exhibits I and 2 were produced by the plaintiff from his own custody and in a case where the plaintiff claims title in the benami the defendant the sale certificate is the most vital and material document and the sale certificate of the instant case along with the writ of delivery of possession were produced by the plaintiff from his own custody. The cases referred to and relied on by Mr. Chowdhury in connection with interpretation of section 66 of the code of civil procedure it is found that in some of those decisions it was also held that the sale certificate is the most vital document and we find that in the instant case not only the sale certificate but also the writ of delivery of possession was produced by the plaintiff from his own custody. 

16. In enumerating the elements of the benami transaction in the case of Nurjahan Begum Vs. Mahmudur Rahman Mollick reported in 34 D. L. R. (AD) 61, our Appellate Division observed that in a benami transaction source of purchase money is an important criteria but it is not conclusive. The source of consideration money though an important criteria in a benami transaction, but in the absence of an unambiguous ownership consideration of that relevant circumstances be come important in a case where ownership is disputed. The disputed question of benami cannot be determined only in the consideration of source of consideration money, and it becomes incumbent for the court to fall back upon the surrounding circumstances of the transaction, the position of the parties and the relationship to each other and the motive which could govern their actions but their subsequent conduct including their dealings and the enjoyment of the property become relevant factors for consideration. Although the course of 'purchase money is an important criteria, but is not concluding where there are other circumstances showing that the purchaser intended property to belong to the person in whose favor the sale deed is executed. So it is the intention of the par-ties which practically determines the question as to who is the owner of the property and where there are benami transaction, and the question is who is the real owner, the actual possession or receipt or rents of the property is most important. On a perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial court we find that both the courts below con-currently found that the plain-tiff opposite party No. 1 got the suit land in auction sale through the principal defendant No. 1 with his own money and for his own benefits and it is not disputed even by the contesting defendants that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 was not a man of sufficient means. 

16(a). It appears from the testimony of P. W, 1 the plaintiff, that he is a graduate of 1941 and the was serving in the Imperial capital at New Dellhi in 1942 and thereafter he came back to his own village in 1961 and started residing at his village home. Similarly both the courts below on evidence concurrently found that the plaintiff opposite party No. I is in possession of the suit land since auction purchase. To prove his possession the plaintiff Opposite party No. 1 examined himself as P. W. I and he testified that he is in possession of the suit land since auction purchase and he has been corroborated on this point by P. Ws. 2 and 3 and not only that even the D. W. I. who is one of con-testing defendants admitted in his cross examination that- নালিমী পুকুরের উপর পাড় সামান্য সেখানে বাদীর বাড়ি আছে " Similarly D.W. 2 Admitted that"  বাদীকে নালিশী পুকুরের পাড়ে আমার জন্মের পূর্ব হইবে বসত বাড়ীতে বসবাস করতে দেখি। নালিশী পুকুর বাদী ব্যবহার করে। and D. W. 3 though stated that the plaintiff uses the suit pond but again stated that the plaintiffs do not catch the fish of the suit pond but this witness admittedly is a bharatie under the defendant Surrender and as such his testimony has been disbelieved by the appellate court below as he is an interested witness. 
16(b). It appears from the impugned judgment that to arriving at a finding on the point of possession the trial court as well as the appellate Court below took into consideration the evidence of all the P. Ws. D. Ws. In this case it appears that the two challenges by which auction money was deposited were produced by the defendant petitioners which were marked as exhibits "Ka" and "Ka" (1) and this documents also considered by both the courts below in arriving of a finding on the point of possession. In a benami Transaction the sale certificate the most important document and in the instant case that document come from the custody of the plaintiff Opposite party No. 1 P. S. Khatian stands in the name of the benamder but the B. S. Khatian stands in the name of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 it is also alleged by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 that the defendant No. 1 is his relative and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 also stated the motive of purchasing the land in the benami of the defendant No. 1. It further appears, from a perusal of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment of the trial court that both the courts below dis-believed the story of the contesting defendant that their predecessor in interest Negendra Lal. Barua purchased the suit land in the benami of the principal defendant No. 1 on the ground that it is admitted by the D. W. 1 that late Nogendra Lal Barua the predecessor in interest of the defendant petitioners were residing of Assam at the relevant time and his uncle also was laying in Barua. His father Negendra Lal Barua Came to this country from Assam in 1961 and died in this coquetry in 1962 but he could not such and passport of his father or death certificate  prove that his father died in this country as alleged by him. It is asserted by the defendant that his father was in possession on the suit land after the auction purchase but admittedly till 1961 his father was serving in Assam. In that view of the matter also both the courts below rightly held that the defendant petitioners failed to prove their possession in the suit land. 

17. In view of my aforesaid discussions it appears to me that though both the courts below did not elaborately dis-cussed about the 4 elements on the benami transaction but nevertheless it appears that in fact both the courts below took into consideration the elements enumerated in the decision reported in 34 D. L. R (AD) 61 and after taking into consideration the material and evidence on record both the courts below have rightly arrived at a con-current finding that the defendant No. 1 was benamder of the plaintiff No. 1. 

18. The next submission of Mr. Chowdhury is that in decreeing the suit both the courts below failed to notice the fact the suit was undervalued 1. e. the suit was not properly valued and for this purpose he relies on section 8(c) of the court fees Act. as Against that Mr. Datta sub-mitted that it is a case of simple declaration and the plaintiff alleged that he is in possession and as such in the instant case no question of advalorem court fee is required. The learned Advocate further submitted that since there is no objective standard for determining the valuation of the declaration sought for by the plaintiff no objection can be taken as to the valuation of the suit itself. It appears from the written statement that the contesting defendant took the objection in their writ-ten statement that the suit has not been properly valued but no such issue was framed by the trial court. The defendants did not bring it to the notice of the trial court that an issue should be framed as to the valuation of the suit but they did not does so nor did they move the higher court for not farming such an issue, It further appears that in the memorandum of appeal that ground no 18 was with regard to the valuation of the suit but from the perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the said ground was not argued at the time of hearing in the revisional application also there is no such statement that they urged the point before the appellate court but the appellate court did not Consider it. In that view of the matter I find substance in the submission made by Mr. Datta and the contesting defendants at this stage cannot be allowed to raise an objection as to valuation of the suit because they slept over the matter after raising the same objection in their written statement, Moreover it is found by both the courts below that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is in possession of the suit land. In a suit for simple declaration the valuation of the suit loses its importance as no question of advalorem court fee is involved when a party being in possession of the suit land prays for mere declaration the valuation of the declaration practically depends of the subjective satisfaction of the plaintiff. 

19. In the course of replying to the submissions of Mr. Datta, Mr. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners submitted that it is apparent or crystal clear the both the courts below did not consider certain documents namely exhibit 'Uma' serious, exhibit"Ga"Cha', Ja Newa as well as exhibit '4' and he also submitted that the finding of the appellate court below on the point of possession also suffers from misreading of evidence inasmuch as the appellate court below found that D. W. 1 and 2 admitted the possession of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 in the suit land but from reading of the evidence, of these 2 (two) D.Ws it would be evident that they stated that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has his homestead not in the bank of the tank but adjacent to the bank of the tank. 

20. In the case of Abdul Mannan and others Vs. Akram Ali and others reported in 43 D.L.R. (AD) 125, it has been held by their Lordships of the Appellate Division that when both oral and documentary evidence are available on record, it is not proper for High Court Division to send back the case on remand rather the High Court Division itself should dispose the matter. This principle has been further clarified by the case of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Aslam and others reported in 44 D.L.R. 69 wherein it has been laid down that with the repeal of section 100 of the code of civil procedure and re-enactment of section 115 of the' code of civil procedure in its new garb, the powers of the High Court' Division has increased to a large extent. Now under the newly amended provision as made in section 115 of the civil procedure code, the grounds for interference has been stretched from jurisdiction all point of view for stretching and superseding the errors on the face of the record into errors of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The strict binding effect of concurrent findings of facts however erroneous the same might Le in revision, the same could not be interfered with has been diminished to a large extent by introducing the words. "error in the decision" complied with occasioning a failure of justice would lead the High Court Division to a larger scope of jurisdiction in mitigating the causes of failure of justice. Now the High Court Division in the interest of justice may go into the question of fact in revision to a limited sense to ameliorate the injustice that the Subordinate Court might commit occasioning failure of justice. The term occasioning failure of justice has a far reaching significance. It invests the High Court Division with wide power not only to go into the question of law but also to the question of fact in search of fact and to make scrutiny and analyze and if necessary to assess evidence for itself for its own satisfaction, how to what extent such failure justice has been perpetrated. In view of latest position as enunciated in those two decisions have no other alternative but to consider the submission made by the learned Advocates for the parties and to see what is the effect of non-consideration of these documents by the courts below. I have 
pursued the entire records of the case including all the documents exhibits exhibited by the respective parties. It appeal from the judgment of the trial court that he has considered all the 
exhibits of both the parties although in so many words he did not discuss about the exhibits mentioned by Mr. Chowdhury, So it cannot be said all there that the trial court did not examine the documents maintained by the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners. 

21. It appears from a perusal of the impugned judgment that the documents mentioned by Mr. Chowdhury has not been discussed in so many words but Have perused all these documents myself. The case of the plaintiff opposite party No.1 is that the defendant No. I was benamder in the auction purchase and plaintiff opposite party No. 1 was the real owner and to prove that he has produced exhibit 1, the sale certificate and exhioit 2, the writ of delivery of possession and both the courts below relying on these two documents along with the other documentary evidence namely exhibit "ka" and "ka" (1) and the rent receipts exhibit "3" and the khatian have arrived at a finding that the principal defendant No. 1 was a mere,: name lander and the plaintiff opposite party no. 1 was the real owner. I have already mentioned earlier that in a benami transaction the sale certificate is the most material document to show who is the real owner and in the instant case the said document came from the possession of the plaintiff opposite party no. 1. The contesting defendants put up a counter claim that they are the real owners and the principal defendant No. 1 was their benamder and to show that they relied on , exhibits 'ka' and `ka' (1) the two challans by which the auction money was deposited in the court. The two documents namely exhibit 'ka' and 'ka' (1) were considered by the appellate court below along with the evidence of P.W. 1 that these documents were given to the principal defendant No. 1 and they were stolen from his custody and for this a G.D. entry was lodged with the local police by the plaintiff opposite party no. 1. It is not denied by the contesting defendants that no such G.D. Entry was lodged by the plaintiff opposite party no. 1 but it is the grievance of Mr. Chowdhury that the plaintiff did not produce the certified copy of the said G.D. Entry and as such the appellate court below should not have relied on the testimony of P.W. 1. It appears from record that a G.D. entry was made by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 after those documents were stolen from the custody of principal defendant No. 1. Be that as it may, these facts were considered by the appellate court below and thereafter the appellate court below concurred with the finding of the trial court that the principal defendant No. 1 was the benamder of the plaintiff opposite party no. 1. From a perusal of these documents along with materials and evidence on record 1 am of the opinion that there are sufficient materials and evidence on record to support the findings arrived at by the trial court as well as the appellate court below on this point. 

22. The next grievance of Mr. Chowdhury is that the appellate court below did not consider exhibit '5' series that is the three rent receipts filed by the contesting defendants which show that they paid rent for the suit land for long 18 years. But exhibit '3' shows that the plain-tiff opposite party no. 1 is paying rent for the suit land even after filing of the pre-sent suit. It is true that the plaintiff did not file earlier rent receipts non there is any explanation from his side as to why he failed to produce those rent receipts although it is asserted by him in the plaint that he is possessing the suit land by paying rent to the government. Be that as it may, exhibit 3 shows that the plaintiff opposite party no. 1 is paying rent for the suit land after filing of the instant suit. In this connection we may refer to the decision reported in 36 D.L.R. 127, Wherein it has been held that non payment of rent by tenant furlong is not a ground to draw conclusion that thereby he has lost title, interest and possession of the land. So in my opinion non consideration of exhibit Uma series by the appellate court below did not cause any miscarriage of justice any even if It were considered by the trial court even then it could arrive at a finding at which it has ultimately arrived at. 

23. Another grievance of Mr. Chowdhury is that the appellate court below did not consider exhibit filed by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. I have perused exhibit 4 and the evidence of P.Ws. and it appears from the deposition of P.W.1 before the trial court that he explained as to why exhibit 4 was taken in the name of his uncle. It is a money receipt granted by the labourere who excavated the tank in question and from exhibit 4 it appears that Surendra Lal Barua was the man who paid money to the labourers for re excavating the tank and the plaintiff as P.W.1 stated in his evidence that he was a man of tender age and as such the money receipt was taken in the name of his uncle but the money was paid from his fund and he practically re excavated the tank by the labourers. It is true that in the impugned Judgment there is no elaborate discussion about exhibit 4 but on a perusal of trial courts Judgment it appears that he considered all the exhibits filed by both the parties. It is a case of affirmance of judgment and as such absence of elaborate discussion of all the exhibits by the appellate court do not vitiate the impugned Judgment. The appellate court has fairly dealt with the material evidence on record and also independently assessed the evidence and after due consideration of all the aspects of the case concurred with the findings of the trial court and in that view of the matter mere non consideration of exhibit 4 by the appellate court does not vitiate the impugned judgment. Here it may further be mentioned that I have examined the materials and evidence on record including exhibit 4 and find that the impugned judgment is sustainable in law. 

24. It is true that there is no mentioned in the appellate courts judgment about exhibit kha and Ga exhibit Kha is the original Khatian and exhibit Ga is Khatian No. 134/151 which stands in the name of surendra Lal Barua the certified purchaser who is alleged to be benamder of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 so it is very material who immediately after the auction sale was inducted into possession of the said land. I have already adverted to oral evidence on the point of possession and both the courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff has successfully  proved his possessions. P.S. Khatian stands in the name of defendant No. 1 but the B.S. Khatian has been recorded in the name of the plaintiff opposite party no. 1 So, the latest record of right stands in the name of the plaintiff. Oral evidence coupled with other documentary evidence 
conclusively prove the possession of plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 in the suit land. No doubt P.S. Khatian stands in the name of defendant No. 1 but it is of an significance in a much as it has been conclusively proved by oral evidence that since auction purchase the plaintiff-opposite party is in possession of the suit land. Regarding other exhibits namely exhibit 
"Cha", "Chha" "Ja(1) and "Newa" it can be stated that these documents have no relevance at all in the instant case because exhibit "Cha" is a Challan with regard to some other lands and "Chha" is a deed of relinquishment by Surendra Lal Barua, the principal defendant No. 1 of the 
instant case, regarding other land to the predecessor-in-interest of the contesting defendant Nos. 4-8 and exhibit "Ja" and "Ja(1)" are two post cards which show that Narendra Lal predecessor-in-interest of the contesting defendants used to write letter to the principal defendant No. 1 Exhibit 'Jha' shows that to meat certain expenditure Narendra was unable to send some money and as such proposed to Surendra Barua to arrange to sell certain landed property of Narendra. Exhibit 
"Ja(1)' is another letter which also shows that he further instructed Surendra Lal Barua to arrange the affairs without selling the landed properties. On perusal of these two letters I do not find how these documents are at all relevant to decide the due issues involved in the instant suit. Similarly exhibit "Newa" is an order sheet dated 26-8-33 of a Mortgage suit of the court of 4th Munsif, Patia. Chittagong. It appears that Surendra Lal Barua was the plaintiff and Rajapur was the defendant. In that case the plaintiff filed an application for attachment before Judgment-" which was allowed. How till document is relevant for determining the issue involved in the instant suit as to whether the principal defendant No. 1. I is the benamder or not, is not at all intelligible to me. So, in my opinion non-consideration of exhibits "Cha", "Ja(1)" and "Nawa" do not have any 
bearing in the instant case at all and I am of the opinion that both the courts below have rightly left out those documents from their consideration in deciding the issues involved in the instant case. Exhibit "Ga"-.1 shows that Surendra Lal Barua and others filed on objection against B. S. Khatian which Stands in the name of plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and till the disposal of the suit, the lard remained recorded in the name of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. There is no evidence on record to show that after the objection raised by the defendant petitioners the B. S. Khatian was ultimately canceled and recorded in the name of some one else other then the 
plaintiff opposite party No. 1 so exhibit "Ga" merely shows that an objection has been filed against B. S. Khatian but that does not debar the court to take into consideration the B. S. Khatian Mr. Chowdhury relying on these documents wanted to argue that from these documents at least it appears that with relation to some other landed properties the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant petitioner has purchased the lands in the benami of the principal defendant No. 1 and therefore, the case made out by the contesting defendants in the instant suit should have been believed by the courts below. I have already pointed out that in my opinion also these documents are not very much relevant at all to decide the issues, involved in the instant case. Be that as it may, there are sufficient materials and evidence on record from which the appellate court below could have arrived at a finding in which he has ultimately arrived at. The primary function of this court when sitting under section 115 of the code is to see whether there are sufficient materials and evidence on record to support the findings of the appellate court below. That a different conclusion could be drawn or arrived at by reassessment of evidence is not a ground for interference. On a perusal of the materials and evidence on record I am of the opinion that non consideration of these document do not have any bearing at all on the ultimate result of the instant suit. 

25. One of the grievance of Mr. Chowdhury is that the impugned judgment suffers from misreading of evidence on the point of possession. On a perusal of the impugned Judgment it is crystal clear that the appellate court below considered the evidence of P. Ws. 1, 2 and 3 in this point. The appellate court below did not find any reason to disbelieve the testimonies of these three P. Ws. on a perusal of the evidence of these three P. Ws. it is found that the plaintiff opposite Party No. 1 as P. W. asserted in his deposition that he is in possession of the suit land since auction purchase and he has been aptly corroborated by the other P. Ws. namely P. Ws. 2 and 3 on ton of that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has been by D. Ws. also D. W. 1 who is one of the contesting defendants has admitted in his cross examination "নালিমী পুকুরের উত্তর পাড় সামান্য সেখানে বাদীর নতুন বাড়ী আছে:  D. W. 2 also stated that বাদীকে নালিশী পুকুরের পাড়ে আমার জন্মের পূর্বে হইতে বসতবাড়ীতে বসবাস করিতে দেখি। নালিশী পুকুর বাদী ব্যবহার করে। and in discussing the evidence of D. W. 3 the appellate court below found that he is a baratia of D. W. 1 and as such he is an interested witness. That is why the appellate court below did not rely on the evidence adduced by D. W. 3 on the point of possession. Nevertheless the appellate court below rightly pointed out that this D. W. 3 stated that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. use the pond but again stated that the plaintiff does not catch fish in the suit pond. From this discussion it is crystal clear that in arriving at a finding that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is in possession of the suit land both the courts adverted to the materials on record and it cannot be said that the impugned judgment suffers from misreading of evidence on that point. 

26. It appears to me that both the courts below disbelieved the case of the contesting defendants on another ground also that is that it is an admitted position that the predecessor in interest of the contesting defendants used to live in Assam and he came back to this country in 1961 and died in 1962. But the contesting defendants namely defendant petitioners failed to produce any passport to show that the ever came back from Assam to the then Pakistan in 1961. Similarly they have also failed to produce the death certificate of Narendra Lal Barua to show that he died really in the then Pakistan. Both the court below took the view that since admittedly Norendra Lal Barua was living Assam at the relevant time of Auction purchase and delivery of possession in in pursuance of said auction sale it was not possible on this part to take possession of the suit land. Both the courts below also dis-believed the defence case of taking possession of the suit land by Narandra Lal Barua after his return to this country in 1961 on the ground that they have failed to produce any passport to show that he ever came back to this country and to show that here died in this country in 1962. In view of the materials and evidence on record it cannot be said that this concurrent finding of both the courts below can be assailed on any ground whatsoever. 

27. In view. of my aforesaid discussions regarding non consideration of certain documents and misreading of evidence, I am of the opinion that the impugned judgment cannot be assailed on those grounds. 

28. In view of my aforesaid discussion I do not find any substance in this revisional application. In the result the rule is discharged without any order as to cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, J: This Rule was obtained by the pre-emptce (purchaser) upon making an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 18. 11.98 passed by Subordinate Judge and 2nd Commercial Court at Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 189 of 1998 reversing those dated 21.06.98 passed by First. Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka in pre-emption Case No. 85 of 1988. 

	2. Late Eklas Hossain Khan predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 made an application under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the case land measuring 0.0206 acre of C.S. and S.A. plot No. 565 appertaining to S. A. Khatian No. 612 and Mutation Khatian No. 474/18. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that the case land along with other lands originally belonged to Jogesh Chandra Majumder and others and the C.S. record of rights was accordingly prepared and published in their names. Golam Mortuza Khan, father of the pre-emptor and opposite party Nos. 3-11 purchased 5 kathas of land by registered deed of sale from the said tenants and lived there by constructing dwelling house and on payment of rents on mutation in his own name. Thereafter Golam Mortuza Khan died leaving pre-emptor and opposite party Nos. 3-5 as four sons and opposite party Nos. 6-11 as six daughters and the said heirs possessed the lands jointly by way of inheritance. Opposite party No. 4 by registered deed of sale dated 18.02.88 transferred his share to his brother opposite party No. 3 and delivered possession. Opposite party No. 3 transferred the said land by a deed of sale executed on the same date to the petitioner and the deed of sale was registered on 13.08.88. In spite of the fact that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the joint tenancy no notice was served upon him. The pre-emptor was in possession in the house constructed by him. 

	3. The purchaser-petitioner is a stranger. He was a tenant under opposite party No. 3. The purchaser, having declined to re-convey the lands to the pre-emptor, the pre-emptor was constrained to make the application for pre-emption. 

	4. The purchaser-petitioner appeared and opposed the application for pre-emption by filing a written objection denying the case of the pre-emptor. His main case is, in short, is that the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters got their inherited lands and properties amicably partitioned by a family arrangement executed on 05.05.78. The case land was recorded in the name of the opposite party No. 3 in the Dhaka Municipal Corporation in separate holding. The pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters are paying rents in two separate jamas. The purchasers after purchase of the case land got his name mutated without any objection from any quarter in Mutation Khatian No. 474/18/1 and have been paying rent since then. The price of the land was though settled at Tk. 1,56,000/- and the purchaser paid the said amount of Tk. 1,56,000/- to opposite party No. 3 as consideration but in the sale deed Taka 50,000/- was written as price. 

	5. After purchase the purchaser had invested huge money to construct a semi-pucca building and installation of electricity, WASA and Gas connection. Thereby he had to incura cost of Taka 1,15,000/ -. 

	6. On the pleadings issues framed are whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy, whether the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation, whether there was any improvement made by the purchase and what relief or reliefs the pre-emptor is entitled to. 

	7. During the pendency of the pre-emption case, the pre-emptor died leaving opposite party No.1 and 2 as his sole heirs and legal representatives who were duly substituted. In support of the case of pre-emption, opposite party Nos.1 and 2 examined two witnesses while purchaser examined five witnesses. On behalf of the pre-emptor various documents were adduced which were marked as Exts. 1-6. The papers and documents adduced on behalf of the purchaser were marked as Exts, Ka to Uma. 

	8. On consideration of the evidence on record the trial court held that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the tenancy, that the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation and that there is a proof of development of the case land by purchaser. Upon such view, the trial court dismissed the application for pre-emption. 

	9. On appeal before the District Judge, Dhaka at the instance of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, the appeal was on transfer heard by Subordinate Judge and 2nd Commercial Court at Dhaka. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, the court of appeal below reversed the findings of the trial court and held that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the holding and that the application for pre-emption was not barred by limitation.  

	10. Mr. N. H. Khondker appearing for the purchaser submits that in view of provision of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellate court failed to take into consideration the findings of the trial court and reasons given for those and without considering the evidence on record held that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the tenancy and the application for pre-emption is not barred by limitation. In support of his submission he also cited the cases reported in 5 BLD (AD) 54, 15 BLD (AD) 91, 16 BLD (AD) 197 and 17 BLD (AD) 47. 

	11. The learned Advocate also submits that the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters were separated by amicable partition among them and had been enjoying separate jama since then and the Municipal holding also shows that the pre-emptor was enjoying his share separately in separate holding number. The Court of appeal below therefore, committed serious error of law in riot considering those facts incoming to its decision. I-le further submits that after purchase he also got his purchased land mutated and he has been paying rent through his mutated Khatian since purchase and also staying there after constructing a semi-pucca house and installing all modern utility services, namely, electricity, gas, WASA etc. Even after such independent and separate enjoyment of the purchased land, the finding of the appellate court that tenancy was riot separated is totally misconceived and not sanctioned by any law. 

	12. Lastly, he submits that as per case of the pre-emptor that on taking certified copy of the impugned kabala No. 617 dated 18.02.88 on 16.03.88 he filed the application on 25.09.88, the application for pre-emption is on the face of it is beyond four months and ought to have been held to be barred by limitation and in support of his submission, he cited the decision reported in 4 BLD (AD) 32. He also cited the decision reported in 33 DLR 318 on subdivision of a holding and distribution of rent. Finally, he submits that the judgment and order of the appellate court below are not proper judgment of reversal and, therefore, are liable to be set aside. 

	13. Mr. Abdul Barek Chowdhury appearing for the opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2, submits that only two questions are involved in the case as to limitation and whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy out of which that land was sold. On limitation, he submits that the impugned kabala was finally registered on 13.08.88 and application was filed on 25.09.88 so it cannot be said that application for pre-emption was beyond the time, no matter the certified copy of the application was obtained on 16.03.88. On the issue of locus standi as co-sharer, he submits that as no order of any competent authority could be adduced by the purchaser to show that the tenancy was ever sub-divided and the rents were distributed amongst the co-sharers of the tenancy and as such, no amount of testimony or amicable partition can be taken into consideration to find the joint tenancy was sub-divided and jama was separated and thereby, the pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the tenancy. 

	14. I have gone through the application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon which the above Rule was issued perused the judgments and orders of the courts below, the application for pre-emption under Section 24 and also the written objection filed by the purchaser I have also examined the evidence, both oral and documentary on record. 

	15. It is true, out of the issues framed by the trial court the issues with regard to limitation and whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy out of which the land was sold are raised as the most issues before me. No other issues was pressed for, so let me see whether the judgment and order of the court of appeal below are well founded in law as well as on facts. 

	16. It is not disputed that opposite party No. 4 Golam Mostafa Khan transferred the case land to his brother opposite party No. 3 Moslemuddin Khan by a deed of sale being No. 601 executed on 18.02.88 Ext. 2 the original of which is Ext. Kha. The said deed was ultimately registered on 11.08.88 and on the same day i.e. on 18.02.88 opposite party No. 3 Moslemuddin Khan transferred the very same land to the purchaser Harun-Or-Rashid by another deed of sale being No. 617 Ext. Gha. This deed of sale i.e. deed No. 617 is the subject matter for pre-emption. The deed clearly shows that it was registered on 13.08.88. On the reverse side of the last page of this deed, all the necessary particulars entering the deed in the volume are there in the endorsement. Even after such clear endorsement as to registration on 13.08.88 why the trial court insisted upon further evidence say calling for the volume from the office of the Sub-Registrar is not really understood. I cannot find any doubt or suspicion ever cropped out in the mind of the trial court about this endorsement of registration. Without recording any doubt or suspicion about the registration of the original deed as adduced by the purchaser, I find the insistence of the trial court for calling for the volume is totally misplaced. I do not find from anywhere in the record that the purchaser ever denied that the deed was not registered on 13.08.88. When the deed is registered on 13.08.88, that registration must be under Section 60 of the Registration Act and on registration the pre-emptor becomes entitled to make the application for pre-emption within four months of the said date of registration. It is true, the pre-emptor applied for and obtained certified copy on 16.03.88 as was repeatedly submitted by the learned Advocate for the purchaser and the application for per-emption was filed on 25.09.88 beyond 4 months. This sub-mission is totally misconceived. The pre-emptor is entitled to make the application for pre-emption within 4 months from date of registration and not from the date of receipt of copy of the sale deed. In such view of the facts and also the law, the court of appeal below rightly approached the issue from correct stand point and found that the application for pre-emption was well within four months from the date of registration. The decision cited on this point by the learned Advocate for the purchaser therefore does not help him any way. 

	17. Now, with regard to the locus standi of the petitioner. I have gone through the written objection filed by the purchaser. He has claimed that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the tenancy on three counts. Firstly after the death of Golam Mortuza Khan the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters amicably partitioned their inherited land and properties and they have been possessing their specific share independently and separately since then. Secondly, the land sold belongs to a separate Municipal holding than that of the holding where the petitioner has been living in and thirdly O.P.W. No. 5 wife of opposite party No. 3 Moslemuddin Khan admitted that after the death of her father-in-law the properties were separated amicably and now the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters staying in their separate and independent shares. The purchaser also adduced a D.C.R. Ext. Uma dated 29.02.88 issued by Assistant Tahsilder in respect of a Khatian No. 474/17/1. I have also seen the rent receipts marked as Ext. Uma (1) and Uma (2) showing payment of rents on 17.03.88 and 14.04.90. I have also perused a tax receipt Ext. Uma (3) issued by Dhaka Municipal Corporation showing payment of tax for the year 1988/89 and 1989/90 against holding No. 18/6/C in the name of Harunur Rashid. The purchaser examined himself as O.P.W. No. 1 and he testified that after the death of Golam Mortuza Khan the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters in 1974 amicably partitioned their inherited lands and properties. He also claimed to have got his purchased lands mutated in his name. In cross-examination, he testified that he could not remember whether he got the land mutated before the making of the application for pre-emption. But he was very categorical in deposing that he did not serve any notice upon the pre-emptor or his brothers and sisters because they were living in separate holdings. 

	18. There is no dispute, the property was originally owned and possessed by Golam Mortuza Khan. After his death the petitioner and his three brothers and six sisters opposite parties 3-11 inherited. They are living separately. Now, the question is whether in view of the above facts and the evidence on record can it be said, there was sub-division of the tenancy held by Golam Mortuza Khan and rents were distributed in accordance with law and thereby, the petitioners ceased to be a co-sharer in the joint tenancy and thereby, lost his right of pre-emption. 

	19. Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950 has provided for sub-division of a holding and/or a joint tenancy and distribution of rents. Section 117 reads-

	(1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue Officer may,-

	(a)   
	(b)   
	(c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any, he may consider fair and equitable:

	Provided that no such order shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter provided....

	This provision is applicable for subdivision and distribution of rents in respect of all sorts of lands, agricultural and non-agricultural. Under the above provision, Revenue officer is given the power to subdivide a joint tenancy for the purpose of distribution of rents. Such jurisdiction can only be exercised upon an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants and after service of reasonable notice to the parties concerned to appear, and after hearing them. Following the provisions of the Section, the Revenue officer by an order in writing may direct subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer-tenants and distribution of rents thereof amongst them. 

	No such order of Revenue officer directing subdivision of the joint tenancy held by Golam Mortuza Khan and distributing the rents amongst the co-sharers i.e. the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters has been adduced in this case. The purchaser have categorically stated that before his getting the purchased land mutated, he did not serve any notice upon any heirs of said Golam Mortuza Khan Because, they are living in separate holding. Here, it must be noted that such authority for subdivision of a joint tenancy and the distribution of rents has not been given to any other authority including the Dhaka Municipal Corporation. Mutation of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation to be valid must be based on an order in writing of the Revenue officer concerned making the joint tenancy subdivided and rents distributed. It cannot be other way round. Separate holding number given by a Municipal Corporation cannot replace an order under Section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, so, the heirs of Golam Mortuza Khan must be held to be still enjoying the joint tenancy left by him. Similarly, no amicable partition among the co-sharers even if reached in writing nor even a decree passed in a partition suit allotting different shares to the co-sharers can substitute the order as mentioned in Section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In such view of the legal position as well as the factual position, the court of appeal below was perfectly justified in holding that the joint tenancy of Golam Murtoza Khan was never subdivided and the rents were never distributed amongst his heirs, pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters in accordance with law, and thereby, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a co-sharer in the Joint tenancy left by him. Accordingly, the pre-emptor, Eklas Hossain Khan is a co-sharer in the joint tenancy left by Golam Mortuza Khan. 

	20. In the case of M.A. Rouf Vs. Ahmuda Khatun, 33 DLR (AD) 323, it was clearly held, any subdivision without notice upon co-sharer of a joint tenancy would not affect the right of pre-emption. Moreover, even if a mutation or subdivision is obtained lawfully during the pendency of a proceeding for pre-emption that must be hit by the doctrine of lies pendent under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this case, the purchaser did not adduce any evidence to show when the purchaser got the purchased land mutated in his name. But, Exts Uma series clearly show, those were issued during the pendency of the proceeding for pre-emption. If it is so, such mutation or subdivision is not based on any lawful order of a Revenue officer. Because, the order admittedly obtained without service of notice upon the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters, must be also hit by the doctrine of lies pendent under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In the case of Begum Aisa Rahman Vs. Abdul Basir Bhuiyan, 26 DLR (SC) 58 it was held, subdivision of a holding without notice, on a co-sharer, does not defeat the right of a co-sharer of pre-emption. In the case of Begum Khodeja Akter Vs. Hareza Khatun, 37 DLR (AD) 212 as referred by Mr. N. H. Khondker for the purchaser, the case was remanded by the Appellate Division to the trial court to determine whether the jama was separated or not as none of the courts below held that a joint holding was subdivided or the rents were distributed. In the case of Sunil Krishna Banik Vs. Kailash Chandra Saha (1984) 4 BLD (AD) 320 the Appellate Division held that if an original co-sharer ceases to be a co-sharer of the joint tenancy he cannot apply for pre-emption. The person making the application for pre-emption must have a subsisting interest in the joint tenancy and such interest must continue au through the proceeding of pre-emption in order to be successful to get an order for pre-emption. 

	21. Further case of the purchaser. In the case of Mst. Mohsena Khatun Vs. M/S. Habiba Kneeting Mill (1977) 17 BLD (AD) 47 the authorities cited as mentioned earlier to the effect that while reversing a judgment of the trial court the appellate court is required to reverse the material findings of the trial court with reference to the evidence on record. I have read the judgment of the court of appeal below and also examined the reasons given by it to its findings. I cannot find anything whereby, the court of appeal below may be held to have failed to exercise its jurisdiction and write out judgment as per provision of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

	22. For the reasons as aforesaid, judgment and order of the court of appeal below do not call for any interference in revision by this Division. 

	23. In the result, the Rule is discharged. No order as to costs. The judgment and order of the court of appeal below reversing those of the trial court are confirmed. The application pre-emption made by the predecessor of opposite party No. 1 and 2 under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the impugned deed No. 617 executed on 18.02.88 and registered on 13.03.88 is allowed. 

	24. The ad-interim order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule is re-called and vacated. Send down the records at once.

End.
