full_judgment:
Mr. A. K. Badrul Huq, J: Judgment of volte-face recorded by Appellate Judge in a Title appeal overruling a judgment recorded by learned Trial judge in a Title Suit is under protest in this Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Judgment of reversal had been recorded by learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Judge, Arbitration Court in Title Appeal No.24 of 1993 reversing Judgment passed by learned Additional Assistant Judge, Third Court in Title Suit No.69 of 1991 wherein declaratory decree has been sought in the terms that orders of allotment dated 22.10.1987 and 18.2.1988 by First-Third defendants, Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakhya (hereinafter referred to Rajuk), Chairman, Rajuk and Board of Trustees, Rajuk in respect of 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land in favour of Md. Omar Faruk, Md. Abdul Mosrur and Md. Iqbal are absolutely illegal, fraudulent, ill motivated ultravires and without jurisdiction and those are contrary to prevalent laws of the land as well as Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and plaintiff is entitled to get the land described in schedule to plaint released in his favour.

3. Case of plaintiff Md. Lutfar Rahman as projected in plaint is:

a. Plaintiff had been owner and possessor of property measuring an area of .49 acres, more or less, 26 katas and 14 chattaks of Cadestral Survey plot no.250 (in part) under Mouza Dhanmondi corresponding to State Acquisition plot no.22 and 23 recorded in State Acquisition Khatian No.54. Plaintiff had been exercising ownership and acts of possession on the property including building and all other structures standing thereon peacefully and uninterruptedly.

b. An area of .8385 Ajutangsha of land of Cadestral Survey Plot no.250 (in part) including buildings, structures and fixtures standing thereon and attached 'thereto were acquisitioned by Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and said land vested with Dhaka Improvement Trust (Shortly DIT) now Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakhya (Rajuk) for construction of roads and side development from Airport Road to Sonargaon Road. Acquisition of land and plan and line shown in the said Martial Law Regulation were vague, unspecified and acquisition was not proper and just in the eye of law.

c. No notice was ever served upon plaintiff showing area of land acquired out of acquired .8385 Ajutangsha. No compensation was paid for acquired land. Possession of land had not been taken over by Rajuk. Development works on road had not been carried out. Rajuk violating all provisions during period of Civil Government made a show of taking delivery of possession of land measuring 13 kathas and 7 chattaks and that 13 kathas and 7 chattaks of land was outside acquisition proceeding and that was outside Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986. Plaintiff had been and has been living there with members of his family.

d. 13 katas and 7 chattaks of land was outside acquired land of Rajuk and Rajuk did never exercise possession thereon. Rajuk issued letter of allotment on 22.10.1987 in favour of plaintiff. Plaintiff laid a suit being Title Suit No.69 of 1991 in the Fourth Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka for a declaration that orders of allotment in his favour are illegal, void, ultra vires, without jurisdiction and order of allotment are not operative and not applicable in respect of plaintiff.

e. Out of rest 13 kathas and 7 chattaks of land, 9 kathas, more or less. had been. used for effecting development on road and rest 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land, more or less, had not been at all used and said 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land is suit property. Rajuk created plot no.2 in respect of 4 kathas of land and created plot no.3 in respect of 7 chattaks of land and Rajuk issued letters of allotment dated 22.10.1987 in favour of Omar Faruk and Abul Mosrur in respect of 4 kathas of land and by letter of allotment dated 18.2.1988 allotted rest 7 chattaks of land in favour of Md. Iqbal. Letters of allotment dated 2210.1987 and 18.2.1988 in favour of allottees were absolutely illegal fraudulent, ill motivated, ultra vires, without jurisdiction and against the prevalent law and Rules contained in Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986.

f. Plaintiff by notice dated 31.12.1989 and, thereafter, by a modified notice dated 7.1.1990 issued notice upon 1. Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakhya (Rajuk), 2. Chairman, Rajuk and 3. Board of Trustee asking them to cancel allotments of 4 Kathas and 7 chattaks of land allotted in favour of Omar Faruk and others and release said land in his favour.

g. Said 4 katha and 7 chattaks of land having not been used for purpose specified in Martial Law Regulation no. VIII of 1986 same was to be released and returned back to plaintiff.

4. First-Third defendants resisted plaintiff's case on presentation of written statement raising following contentions amongst other:

a. Plaintiff got no cause of action to institute suit.

b. Suit is barred by limitation

c. Plaintiff's suit is barred by laws and principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence.

d. Suit property vested with Rajuk through Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986.

e. Plaintiff did not lay his claim for compensation within 60 days as contained in sub-section 3 of section 5 of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986.

f. Possession on entire land and part structure of the plaintiff together with other lands of other people were taken over. Roads and land had been developed and plots were allotted to affected parsons for rehabilitation. Structures standing on land had not been dismantled as because plaintiff was rehabilitated there.

g. The plots allotted to persons noted in plaint had been under the purview of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and plaintiff got no legal authority to challenge that.

h. Plaintiff had been allotted plot No. 1 depicting him as affected person.

i. Suit land having vested with DIT under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 question of releasing of land did not at all arise and all steps had been undertaken under Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986.

j. Plot No. 1 had been allotted to plaintiff and plaintiff along with other persons approached the Hon'ble president of the Republic for reduction of price of plot. Plaintiff on 29.09.1988 by way of a petition addressed to Rajuk prayed for handing over the possession of allotted plot no.1 and plaintiff on 5.1.1989 took possession of same.

5. Pleading of parties gave rise to following issues:

1. Was the suit as framed maintainable?

2. Had plaintiff got any cause of action to institute suit?

3. Was the plaintiff entitled to decrees as sought for?

4. What were other relief or reliefs plaintiff was entitled to?

6. Evidences, both oral and documentary, had been led by both parties in support of their respective claims. Plaintiff Md. Lutfar Rahman as PW I examined himself in support of his plaint case. Md. Lutfar Rahman, Deputy Director (in-charge), Land Survey Department, Rajuk stood on witness box in support of defendant's case.

7. Learned Additional Assistant Judge as Trial judge decided all the Issues against plaintiff and in favour of defendants. In deciding Issues learned Trial Judge held:

I. 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land was acquired under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and acquisition matter stood proved by copy of Martial Law Regulation, Exhibit-Ka and Gazette Notification, Exhibit-Kha.

II. It appeared that suit plot nos.2 and 3 had been allotted in favour of three affected persons, by Rajuk. Plaintiff did not receive any compensation money. Suit property 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land had not been returned back to plaintiff and land was allotted in favour of three affected persons under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986. No provision had been embodied in the matter of returning back unused excess land in favour of owner and there had been, also, no provision for giving allotment to other persons fixing higher price and in Regulation no provision had been indicated in the matter of realization of higher price.

III. Government could decide correctness or incorrectness of allotment in favour of three affected persons taking into stock public purposes engrafted in Rule 6 of Regulation No. VIII of 1986. No claim had been put forward by plaintiff in respect of rest 9 kathas of acquired land. Generally, under acquisition and requisition law original owners got back unused acquired land.

IV. On examination of papers and documents of plaintiff and actions taken by Rajuk it appeared that defendant nos. 1-3 under purview of Regulation No. VIII of 1986 sidelined natural justice and applied will force.

V. Officers of Rajuk under garb of Martial Law Regulation acquired suit property of plaintiff and other properties of other persons and subsequently carried on acts of allotment of plots.

VI. Under Regulation No. VIII of 1986 plaintiff was not entitled to have any decree from Court. Learned Trial Judge, thus, dismissed suit.

8. Feeling aggrieved of above adjudication of suit by learned Trial Judge, plaintiff sought  overturning the same through a medium of appeal being Title Appeal No.24 of 1993 before learned District Judge, Dhaka. Learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and, also, Arbitration Judge, Dhaka heard the appeal and by Judgment and decree dated 5.10.1994 allowed appeal, set aside judgment and decree passed by learned Trial Judge. Learned Appellate Judge awarded decree in favour of plaintiff.

9. Learned Appellate Judge in allowing appeal on setting aside Trial Judge's Judgment and decree rendered following decisions:

a. No provision had been contained in Regulation No. VIII of 1986 in the matter of returning back unused property to original owner and at the " same time no provision, also, had been contained in Martial Law Regulation giving allotment to Third party on fixation of higher price.

b. It is recited in Regulation No. VIII of 1986 that Regulation was promulgated only for a particular period and naturally with the withdrawal of Martial Law, Civil Law i.e. Requisition and Acquisition Property Ordinance 1982 would come into force.

c. In spite of non-acceptance of compensation money by plaintiff, defendant acted against natural and prevailing law in allotting acquired property in favour of Third party. Plaintiff laid suit in the year 1990 and unused property had been allotted after withdrawal of Martial Law Regulation in favour of Third person. Plaintiff in consonance with prevailing Civil law of the land, in the interest of justice as original owner was entitled to return back suit property.

d. Learned Trial Judge, though, conceived of all the factors and circumstances yet failed to render justice taking into account Martial Law Regulation as sensitive.

Learned Appellate Judge took into notice of a finding rendered by learned Trial Judge in the language that First-Third defendants under garb of Martial Law Regulation sidelined natural justice and used will-force. Learned Appellate Judge positively held that plaintiff was declared to entitlement of having his property released in his favour. Learned Appellate Judge, thus, decided three issues formulated by him in the Appeal in favour of plaintiff-appellant.

10. Feeling dissatisfied, First-Third defendants as petitioners approached this Court in  this Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code of. Civil Procedure pressing into service following grounds:

I. Court of appeal on misappreciation of evidence and materials on record and on misconception of law most illegally passed judgment and decree causing serious miscarriage of justice.

II. First opposite party having been sufficiently compensated by way of giving allotment of a plot at a lower price in the category of affected person the claim of suit land by him is not sustainable in law.

III. Court of appeal committed an error of law occasioning a failure of justice in passing  impugned judgment and decree having no discussion of any evidence on record and thereby committed an error of law.

IV. First opposite party accepted compensation money by way of adjustment of same with First installment of plot allotted to him and subsequent claim of First opposite party is not sustainable in law.

V. Acquisition having been made under Regulation No. VIII of 1986, court of appeal committed an error of law in failing to hold that such acquisition is immune from challenge before civil court.

11. Plaintiff opposite party Md. Lutfar Rahman offered re-joinder to contents encompassed in Revision Petition on laying Counter-Affidavit.

12. Lifeblood of contents are catalogued hereunder:

a. There is no provision of Regulation No. VIII of 1986 to allot any unused land to any person or persons. Petitioner in utter violation of Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and for pecuniary gain with malafide motive allotted unused acquired land including suit property to alleged affected persons at an exorbitant and higher rate without any development of same.

b. First opposite party did never accept his alleged allotment in plot no. 1 nor he applied to President to reduce price of his alleged allotment in plot no. 1 nor any survey was made nor he took any delivery of possession in plot no.1. Land of alleged plot no. 1 was not acquired under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and petitioner, thus, did not take any possession of same and no compensation money was paid to First opposite party and First-opposite party has been in peaceful and undisturbed possession of land of alleged allotted plot no. I and building standing thereon and has been living there with all his family members. Land and buildings of alleged allotted plot no. 1 have no bearing and any connection whatsoever with suit property of instant case and f. petitioners with a malafide motive tried to create cloud by bringing here the case of alleged allotted plot no. l. Unused and excess land could not be allotted to anybody by petitioner and there is no provision in Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 to give such allotment to any person and First Opposite party got legal right to challenge allotment in favour of allottees Mr. Omar Farook and others. First opposite party is entitled to get back unused and excess acquired suit property as per provision of law of land.

c. Allotted plot was not acquired under Marital Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and it remained in peaceful and undisturbed possession of First opposite party as before.

d. Petitioner in utter disregard and violation of provision of Marital Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 malafidely allotted unused suit property to alleged affected persons with exorbitantly higher rate for its pecuniary gain without any development of same.

e. Suit property including other lands was acquired under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 purely for public recreational purposes and for public purposes and not for rehabilitation of any affected person or persons. Excess and unused acquired land was to be returned to person from whom it was acquired on the strength of section 17 of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982. First opposite party is entitled to get back excess and unused acquired suit property.

f. Alleged allotment of plot no. 1 in favour of First opposite party is a separate issue and got no bearing and connection with present suit. Suit property of present suit measuring 4 kathas and 7 chattaks including other 9 kathas of land was owned and possessed by First opposite party and said land was acquired by Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986. Nine (9) kathas of land was used for the purpose it was acquired, though, compensation money was not paid to First opposite party in spite of repeated reminders and requests. Remaining 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of acquired land was not used for the purpose it was acquired and it became excess and remained unused. Petitioners instead of returning back suit property to this First opposite party, as per provision of law of land allotted suit property i.e. 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land in favour of different persons on the plea of rehabilitation of affected person in utter violation and disregard of provision of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986. Petitioners illegally and without any jurisdiction and authority allotted suit property to other persons on the plea of rehabilitation on commercial point of view at a very higher rate instead of returning the same to First opposite party.

g. There is no provision in Regulation No. VIII of 1986 for adjustment of compensation.

13. In Revision case plaintiff-opposite party Md. Lutfar Rahman having been dead his

heirs had been substituted as opposite party nos. 1 (ka) and 1 (kha).

14. Substituted opposite party nos. 1 (ka) and 1 (kha) by way of Supplementary Affidavit brought before this Court the fact that Standard Lease Agreement for Land had been executed by Rajuk in favour of allottees Md. Omar Faruk and Md. Abdul Masrur on 25.3.2001 and said Standard Lease Agreement for Land is hit by doctrine of Lispendens.

15. Petitioners presented Affidavit-in-reply against Supplementary Affidavit filed by substituted opposite party nos. I (ka) and 1 (kha) incorporating statements, that Md. Lutfar Rahman, predecessor of substituted opposite party nos.l(ka) and I(kha) filed a joint petition before Hon'ble President of Republic on 13.5.1988 for reducing registration cost and refixing the value of land-hold plots and Md. Lutfar Rahman on 29.9.1988 submitted a petition to Deputy Director, Rajuk requesting him to handover possession of plot no.1.

16. In this Judgment defendants-petitioners shall be depicted as petitioners and substituted opposite parties shall be known as opposite parties.

17. Sustainability of decisions reached by learned Appellate Judge has been attacked by petitioners pressing into service Five branches of contentions and contentions so advanced have been repelled from side of opposite parties.

18. First branch of contention moved forward from side of petitioners is that suit property vested with Rajuk under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and plaintiff was barred by law to challenge vesting under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and plaintiff was barred by law to challenge the vesting and acts and action taken by Rajuk under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 is protected by Seventh Amendment of The Constitution of the People's Republic 'of Bangladesh and suit as framed was not maintainable.

19. Countering said contention argument had been put forward in bringing home contention from side of opposite parties that plaintiff did not at all challenge vires of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and he had challenged legality of two orders of allotment in favour of Md. Omar Faruk and two others by two letters dated 22.10.1987 and 18.2.1987 and, also, sought declaratory decree in terms that plaintiff was entitled to have suit property released in his favour.

20. Proclamation of Martial Law was made on March 24, 1982. Martial Law Regulation No, VIII of 1986 was promulgated on August 4, 1986. Martial Law was withdrawn by a Proclamation on November 10, 1986. Seventh Amendment of The Constitution had been passed by Parliament on November 11, 1986 ratifying and confirming Martial Law of Proclamation dated 24th March, 1982 and all other Proclamations, Orders, Instructions and Ordinances and all other laws made during period between 24th March, 1982 and date of commencement of Seventh Amendment of Constitution amended on November 11, 1986. All orders made, act and things done and actions and proceeding taken during said period i.e. 24.3.1982-11.11.1986 had been deemed to have been validly made, done or taken and protection given by Seventh Amendment of Constitution was in respect of orders, acts and things done and actions and proceeding taken during said period i.e. 24.3.1982-11.11.1986.

21. Letters of allotment dated 22.10.1987 and 18.2.1988 had not been issued during life time of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and those were issued long after withdrawal of Martial Law and when Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was not in existence and same faced legal death by Proclamation withdrawing Martial Law and, also, after the passing of Seventh Amendment of Constitution on November 11, 1986. Impugned letter of allotment were issued on the strength and reference of dead Martial Law Regulation and those are outside the purview of protection protected by Seventh Amendment and letters under challenge in suit are not safeguarded by Seventh Amendment of Constitution. Contention surged forward from side of petitioners in respect of protection by Seventh Amendment carries no force.

22. Suit property which is 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land along with 9 kathas of land had  been acquired as land of plaintiff and land acquired and vested with Rajuk under Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was for specified purposes as enshrined in Rule 6 which enjoined that land would be used by Trust for construction of roads and highways and for development for commercial and public recreational purposes and for such other public purposes as Trust might in consultation with Government decide. Land acquired was to be used-only for specified purposes noted in Rule 6 of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and for' no other purposes land could be used. Words "for development for commercial and public recreational purposes" means development for purposes, both commercial and public. Commercial recreation is for a community of people land not for a particular person or persons. Letters of allotment in favour of allottees Md. Omar Faruk and two others could not be said to be allotment for commercial and recreational public purposes but for personal benefits of allottees Md. Omar Faruk and others and allotments were against spirit of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986. Letters of allotment had been challenged in suit and it cannot be at all suggested that suit was not maintainable as canvassed from side of petitioners. First branch of contention advanced from side of petitioners having been devoid of any substance stands rejected.

23. Second branch of contention advanced is that plaintiff suit was not maintainable in a Civil Court and civil court got no jurisdiction to try plaintiff’s suit. Sub-rule 1 of Rule 5 of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 has been referred to in support of contention.

24. Contention so pressed has been countered in raising counter contention that Civil  court retained jurisdiction to entertain and try any suit to examine whether provisions contained in any Statute, Ordinance and Regulation had been complied with or not and defendants Rajuk in total disregard of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 issued impugned two letters of allotment dated 22.10.1987 and 18.2.1988 in favour of Md. Omar Faruk and two others and, also, when Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was not in existence and faced legal death and letters had been issued on the strength and reference of dead Martial Law Regulation and Civil Court, thus, retained jurisdiction to entertain and try suit.

25. Sub-Rule 1 of Rule 5 of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 postulate that save  as provided in this Regulation, no person shall be entitled to any compensation from the said Trust or from any other person for the vesting in the said Trust of the scheduled land or any part thereof under this Regulation or for his dispossession or eviction therefrom and no court shall entertain any suit, petition or application where such vesting, dispossession or eviction is called in question or any prayer for such compensation has been made.

26. Ouster clause had been provided in respect of a suit calling in question vesting, dispossession or eviction or any compensation made under Martial Law Regulation. Challenge to two allotment letters in favour of Md. Omar Faruk and two others did not come under ouster clause. Positive case programmed in plaint was that plaintiff had been in exclusive possession on suit property and plaintiff had never been dispossessed and evicted from any portion of suit property. Plaintiff did not challenge vesting, dispossession and eviction and as such Sub-Rule 1 of Rule 5 of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 could not be at all attracted to suit laid by plaintiff.

27. Impugned letters were dated 22.10.1987 and 18.2.1988 which were after withdrawal of Martial Law and when Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was not in force and even after passing of Seventh Amendment of Constitution by Parliament. Suit was filed on 6.3.1990. Under Seventh Amendment of Constitution, all orders made, acts and things done and actions taken under Martial Law Regulation was deemed to have been validly made, done or taken and those were not to be challenged before any Court or Tribunal and suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding in any Court, Tribunal against any person or authority for or on account of or in respect of any order made, act or thing done or action or proceeding taken whether in exercise or purported exercise of powers referred to in Sub- Paragraph (2) had been barred. Since impugned letters had been issued after withdrawal of Martial Law and when Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was not in force and when suit was filed long after withdrawal of Martial Law and on legal funeral of Martial Law Regulation, there could not be any attraction of Sub-Rule 1 of Rule 5 of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and there could not be any safeguard under Seventh Amendment of Constitution.

28. Law is well settled that even if jurisdiction of a Civil Court is excluded still Civil Court got jurisdiction to examine into cases where provisions of any Act, Ordinance, Regulation etc. have been complied with or not and Statutory Authority/Tribunal has not acted in conformity with provisions embodied in Statute, Ordinance and Regulation. Secretary of State Vs. Mask and Company, AIR 1940 PC 105 is a basic authority on this point. Principle stated by Judicial Committee of Privy Council in the above well-known case had been couched in the following language:

"It is settled law that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is not to be readily inferred, but that such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. It is also well settled that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure".

The great principle of law has been consistently followed by Superior Courts of this Sub- Continent and the principle still holds good. Impugned letters having been nullity and coram non-judice, Civil Court got the jurisdiction to entertain and try suit. Second branch of contention pressed into service from side of petitioners is devoid of any substance and holds no water at all.

29. Third branch of contention advanced from side of petitioners is that suit is hit under provision of section 42 of The Specific Relief Act and plaintiff did not acquire any legal character to seek relief or reliefs as sought by plaintiff.

30. Section 42 of Specific Relief act enshrines that any person entitled to any legal character. or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the Court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any

further relief:

Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title omits to do so.

31. The object of section 42 of Specific Relief Act is to perpetuate and strengthen testimony regarding title of plaintiff so that adverse attacks on it may not weaken it. "Legal character" has been taken to mean "Legal Status", a phrase known to Jurisprudence. A man's status or legal character is constituted by attributes which the law attaches to him in his individual and personal capacity.

32. Case projected by plaintiff in plaint was that out of 26 and 14 kathas of land, 13 kathas and 7 chattaks of land was outside acquired land of Rajuk and 13 kathas and 7 chattaks of land was acquired land. Out of 13 kathas and 7 chattaks of land, 9 kathas more or less had been used for effecting development of road and 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land more or less had not been at all used and said 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land had been and has been in possession of plaintiff. Rajuk created plot no.2 in respect of 4 kathas of land and created plot no. 3 in respect of 7 chattaks of land and allotted 4 katas of land in favour of Md. Omar Faruk and Abdul Masrur and allotted 7 chattaks of land in favour of Md. Iqbal. Plaintiff s assertion that 13 kathas and.7 chattaks of land including unused 4 kathas and 7 chattacks of land had been acquired for the purpose detailed in Rule 6 of Martial Regulation No. VIII. of 1986 and the purposes were for construction of roads and highways and for development for commercial and public recreational purposes and for such other public purposes as the said Trust might in consultation with the Government decide. Allotment of 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land in favour of allottees Md. Omar Faruk and two others were absolutely illegal, void and contrary to Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986. 4 kathas and 7 chattaks of land having been unused land, plaintiff in the capacity of original owner of said land was entitled to have property released and by allotments in favour of Md. Omar Faruk and two others right of plaintiff to the said 4 katas and 7 chattaks of land had been infringed and plaintiff, thus, got legal character and legal status to file and maintain suit. It, thus, cannot be said that suit is barred under provision of section 42 of Specific Relief Act. Third branch of contention having been bereft of substance stands spurned.

33. Fourth branch of contention pressed into service is that plaintiff by way of a letter dated 29.9.1988 offered request to Deputy Director, Rajuk to handover possession of plot no. I. in his favour and plaintiff along with other affected person made representation to President in the matter of reduction of price- of allotted plot and President Secretariat received representation on 13.5.1988 and plaintiff's claim on suit property is barred by laws and principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence.

34. Contention so raised has been repelled from side of opposite parties in advancing counter contention that subject matter of instant suit was in respect of plot no.2 and 3 created by Rajuk for the purpose of allotment and alleged letters addressed to Deputy Director, Rajuk was for alleged handing over possession of created plot no. 1 and alleged representation to President in respect of reduction price was, also, in respect of said created plot no. 1 and those got no bearing and nexus in the instant suit.

35. In paragraph no. 10 of Written statement it had been stated that plot no.1 had been allotted to plaintiff and plaintiff along with other persons presented a petition before Hon'ble President for reduction of price and President reduced price and plaintiff on 29.9.1988 by way of a petition offered request to defendants Rajuk to hand over possession of plot no. 1 in his favour and final survey had been effected on the allotted plot. DW I, the lone witness for defendants Rajuk made disclosure in his evidence that plaintiff laid petition to President for reduction of price of allotted plot and petition had been exhibited as Exhibit-Ga and plaintiff on 29.9.1988 filed a petition before Rajuk for handing over possession of allotted plot in his favour and the petition had been exhibited as Exhibit No. "Gaha".

36. Photocopy of letter allegedly written by plaintiff Md. Lutfar Rahman to Deputy Director, Rajuk in the matter of handing over of possession was in respect of plot no. 1 (Exhibit- Gaha) and photocopy of letter allegedly sent by plaintiff Md. Lutfar Rahman along with other six persons to Hon'ble President of Republic (Exhibit-Ga) was, also, in respect of allotted plots including plot no.1 allegedly allotted to plaintiff Md. Lutfar Rahman.

37. In schedule of plain of Title Suit No. 69 of 1991 plot nos. 2 and 3 of Rajuk lay out plan had been made schedule land. Exploration of letter dated 29.09.1988 allegedly written by plaintiff Md. Lutfar Rahman to Deputy Director, Rajuk and also alleged representation by way of a letter allegedly made by plaintiff and other six persons to President of Republic was for alleged allotted plot no. 1 and other plots and Exhibits-Ga and Gaha, thus, got no nexus and bearing in of disposal of suit wherein schedule land described in the plaint had been plot nos.2 and 3 of Rajuk layout plan. Contention so advanced from side of petitioners does not appear to have carry any force and same stands ruled out.

38. Fifth branch of contention canvassed from side of petitioners is that Appellate Judge did not at all reverse findings arrived at by Trial Judge and Judgment cannot be characterized to be a proper judgment of reversal and that judgment got no leg to stand.

39. Repelling the said contention it had been contended from side of opposite parties that Appellate Judge in rendering his decision took into account provisions of law contained in Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and, also, section 17 of The Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 (II of 1982) and, also, fact and circumstances of the case and ultimate conclusion reached by Appellate Judge cannot be taken of any exception and same is well merited. Learned Trial Judge in dismissing suit rendered some contradictory and conflicting decisions and by contradictory and conflicting decisions the merit of decision of suit had been seriously affected, it has been further submitted.

40. Examined carefully judgments recorded both by Trial Judge as well as Appellate  Judge, Careful examination of judgment indicates that Trial Judge rendered some conflicting decisions and he had blown hot and cold. Learned Trial Judge held that no provision had been embodied in the matter of returning back unused excess land in favour of owner and there had been, also, no provision giving allotment to other person fixing higher price and in Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 no provision had been manifested in the matter of realization of higher price. Learned Trial Judge, also, found that generally under Acquisition and Requisition law original owners got back unused acquired land. Learned Trial Judge, thereafter, found that on examination of papers and documents, of plaintiff and actions taken by Rajuk it appeared that defendant nos.1-3 under purview of Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 sidelined natural justice and applied will force. Decisions reached by Trial Judge appeared to have suffered from legal infirmity. Appellate Judge in allowing appeal found that no provision had been contained in Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 in the matter of returning back unused property to original owner and at the same time no provision had been, also, contained in Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 in giving allotment to Third party on fixation of higher price. Appellate Judge, also, held that Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was promulgated only for a particular period and naturally with the withdrawal of Martial Law, Civil Law i.e. Acquisition and Requisition Property Ordinance of 1982 (II of 1982) would come into force. Learned judge again found that in spite of non-acceptance of compensation money by plaintiff defendant acted against natural and prevailing law in allotting acquired property in favour of Third Parties and plaintiff laid suit in the year 1990 and unused property had been allotted after withdrawal of Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 in favour of Third persons. Learned Appellate Judge, also, rendered decision that plaintiff in consonance with the prevailing Civil law of the land, in the interest of justice as original owner, was entitled to have the suit property returned back and Trial Judge failed to render justice taking into account Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 as sensitive.

41. Both plaintiff and defendants put on witness box one witness on each side. True it is that learned Appellate Judge did not discuss the evidences of plaintiff witness (PW1) and defendant witness (DWI) threadbare but it cannot be said that learned Appellate Judge did not at all consider pleadings of parties, fact and circumstances of the case and, also, relevant laws in resolving the controversy. Learned Appellate Judge, also, took into account the question of natural justice and, also, took a view of all pictures and fact and circumstances disclosed. Ultimate conclusion reached by Appellate Judge in awarding decree in favour of plaintiff cannot be subjected to any exception and ultimate conclusion appears to be sound, reasoned, well merited and articulated. It, thus, cannot be suggested that Judgment of Appellate Judge reversing decisions rendered by Trial Judge suffers from gross illegality, legal infirmity and perversity warranting any interference by this Court in the exercise of Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged under section 115 of The Code.

42. Great emphasis had been laid from side of opposite parties that suit property i.e. 4  kathas and 7 chattaks of land was acquired from ownership of plaintiff and that land was very much unused land. By impugned allotments by two letters it was manifestly clear that land was unused land and Rajuk did never exercise any acts of possession and on withdrawal of Martial Law, Law of Land i.e. The Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 (11 of 1982) came into picture and that law was very much applicable in respect of releasing of suit property in favour of plaintiff.

43. Strenuous argument had been put forward from side of petitioners that since land was acquired and vested with Rajuk, plaintiff could hot put forward any claim in the matter of returning back or releasing said land and plaintiff's claim in respect of returning back or releasing the same .land in his favour is to be turned down. In support of his contention Al- Haj Abul Basher being dead his heirs Hosne-Ara Begum and others Vs. Bangladesh and others, 50 DLR AD 11 has been relied upon in support of argument.

44. Before adverting to authority relied upon it is posited that a decision is only an authority for what it actually decides and it cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every Judgment must be made applicable to particular facts proved or assumed to be proved and generality of expression that may be found cannot be intended to be exposition of whole law but must be regarded as governed or qualified by the particular facts of the case in which such expression occurs.

45. In Al-Haj Abul Basher being dead his heirs Hosne-Ara Begum and others Vs. Bangladesh and others (Supra) original owners had already received 90% of their compensation and only 10% remained unpaid and after getting 90% compensation money they claimed release of requisitioned property on the basis of Inter-Ministerial Communication. In the said case it has been held that no legal and vested right accrued in favour of petitioner by mere Inter-Ministerial Communication and petitioner could not have any legal right to ask for return of land.

46. In the case in hand plaintiff asserted that no compensation money had been given to him and he did not receive any compensation money whatsoever. No paper and no document had been produced from side of petitioners Rajuk evidencing that any compensation had been paid to plaintiff. DW 1 who was the only witness for defendant Rajuk standing on witness box blurted out that plaintiff did not put forward any claim nor did present any petition before Deputy Commissioner for compensation according to Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986. In view of positive evidence coming from the mouth of DW 1 who is no other than the Deputy Director-in-charge (Land), Rajuk, the point had been very much crystalized that no compensation money had been paid to plaintiff. In Al-Haj Abul Basher being dead his heirs Hosne-Ara Begum and others Vs. Bangladesh and others (Supra), 90% of compensation money had been withdrawn by petitioner but in the case in hand no compensation money at all had been withdrawn by plaintiff. The fact and circumstances of the cited case is quite distinguishable in the fact and circumstances of the case in hand and got no bearing at all. Petitioners cannot have any benefit from the case cited.

47. Only question now survives for determination is whether plaintiff can be graced with  a declaratory decree in the matter of entitlement to have suit property released in his favour on declaring allotments given to Md. Omar Faruk and others by way of two impugned letters to be illegal, void, malafide, ultravires and without jurisdiction and whether the decision reached by learned Appellate Judge warrants any interference by this Court in the exercise of its discretionary Revisional Jurisdiction envisaged in section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure.

48. Admittedly, suit land i.e. 4 kathas and 7 chattacks of land, though, acquired by   petitioners Rajuk but same remained unused. Purposes listed in Rule 6 of Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 for the acquisition of land under Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 were not at all materialized and said land was not used for construction of roads and highways and for development for commercial and public recreational purposes and for other public purposes and the same was very much evident from allotments bestowed upon allottees Md. Omar Faruk and others.

49. Allotments on the strength of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 were made when Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986 was not in existence with the withdrawal of Martial Law. With the withdrawal of Martial Law there had been legal death of Martial Law Regulation No. VIII of 1986. Country was controlled by Civil Law and Civil Government and Administration had been functioning. With the withdrawal of Martial Law, Civil Law which is the Law of the land in respect of any acquisition and requisition of any immovable property The Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 (II of 1982) took the

field. Allotments provided to allottees Md. Omar Faruq and others on the strength and reference of dead Martial Law Regulation when Ordinance II of 1982 was in operation are nullity and coram nonjudice. Section 17(2) of The Ordinance of 1982 postulates that if any requiring person used any acquired property in contravention of the Ordinance of sub-section 1 or does not use it for the purpose for which is acquired he shall be liable to surrender property to Deputy Commissioner on being directed by him to do so. Suit was filed on 6.3.1990 and on that date Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 (11 of 1982) was very much in the field and provision engrafted in section 17(2) of The Ordinance of 1982 was and is very much applicable in respect of release of suit property.

50. Admittedly, suit property was not used nor utilized by Requiring body Rajuk and suit property is required to be returned back on releasing it to plaintiff and on the death of plaintiff his heirs the opposite parties now acquired the entitlement to have the suit property released or returned back in their favour.

51. Since suit property is the acquired property of plaintiff, natural justice, fair play and equity demands that suit property be returned back to heirs of plaintiff the opposite party Nos.1 (ka) and 1 (kha) on its release.

52. Learned Appellate Judge on consideration of materials on record and taking into stock and ruminating relevant laws such as Martial Regulation No. VIII of 1986 and Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 (11 of 1982) and fact and circumstances of the case delivered verdict decreeing the suit on overturning decisions rendered by learned Trial Judge.

53. Exploration of decisions and reason leading to conclusion by Appellate Judge in

granting relief to plaintiff it does not appear to have suffered from patent wrongness,

dodderiness and waywardness. Decisions and reasons leading to decisions and ultimate conclusion reached by Appellate Judge are discreet, prudent and judicious.

<u>54. It is well settled that decisions whether affirmance or reversal reached by Appellate Judge are not open to interference by High Court Division in exercise of Revisional jurisdiction contemplated in section 115 of The Code unless it is shown that decisions are founded on misconception or misapplication or misapprehension of law or any misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise those are perverse being contrary to law, evidence and materials on record. It is, also, well recognized that Jurisdiction of High Court Division while hearing a Revision Petition is purely discretionary and discretion is to be exercised only when there is an error of law resulting in an error in the decision and by that error a failure of justice has been</u>

<u>occasioned and interference is called for the end of justice and not otherwise. Error in the decision of Sub-ordinate Courts do not by itself justify interference in Revision unless it is manifested that by the error substantial injustice has been rendered. Decision which is calculated to advance substantial justice is not to be interfered in Revision. A study of the decisions rendered, reason assigned in rendering decisions and conclusion reached by Appellate Judge does not come into sight that those had been founded on any misconception, misapplication and misapprehension of law or misinterpretation of any material document or otherwise those were wrong headed and by those decisions and conclusion a failure of justice has been occasioned warranting interference by this Court in exercise of Revisional Jurisdiction engrafted in section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

55. This takes me to contention addressed from side of opposite parties that Standard Lease Agreement for Land in favour of Md. Omar Farook and Md. Abdul Masrur is hit under the doctrine of Lis Pendens embodied in section 52 of The Transfer of Property Act.

56. The contention so pressed from side of opposite parties has not been resisted from side of petitioners by way of counter contention.

57. Section 52 enacts the doctrine of Lis Pendens which is expressed in the maxim "ut  pendente nihil innovetur". The doctrine is derived from rules of jus gentium which became embodied in Roman Law where there is the maxim: Ram (sic) de qua controversia probibemur

(sic) in acrum dedicare which means a thing concerning which there is a controversy is prohibited, during the suit, from being alienated.

In the Corpus Juris Secundum Vol. LIV, Page 570 the definition is stated thus:

"Lis pendens literally means a pending suit; and the doctrine of lis pendens has been defined as the jurisdiction, power, or control which a court acquires over property involved in a suit pending the continuance of the action, and until final judgment therein."

<u>58. Section 52, thus, enjoins that during the pendency in any Court in Bangladesh any suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose. It is intended by this provision of law to protect the parties to the litigation against alienation by the opposite parties during the pendency of the litigation. But it is well recognized that the effect of section 52 of Transfer of Property Act is not to wipe out a sale pendentelite altogether but to subordinate it to the rights based on the decree or the order passed in the proceeding. The pendentelite takes the property subject to the result of the suit or proceeding. It is to be noticed that the right under the decree or order is sought to be protected by the doctrine of lis pendens. B u t if the proceeding cannot yield any result creating any right in favour of a party to the proceeding, the question of applying the Doctrine does not arise.</u>

59. Standard Lease Agreement for Land dated 20.3.2001 between Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakhhya (Rajuk) and Md. Omar Farook and Md. Abdul Masrur has been annexed as  Annexure' A' to Supplementary Affidavit presented by opposite parties. Letters of allotment in respect of plot no.2 of layout plan of Rajuk in favour of Md. Omar Farook and Md. Abdul Mosrur leading to Standard Lease Agreement for Land for the said plot no.2 had been under challenge in suit by plaintiff. Appellate Judge on overturning Judgment of Trial Judge decreed the suit in favour of plaintiff. Defendants Rajuk questioned propriety, of Judgment and decree of Appellate Judge on bestowing Civil Revision Petition. Suit had been filed on 6.3.1990. Judgment of Appellate Judge was delivered on 5.10.1994. Civil Revision under section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure had been laid on 29.1.1995 and Rule was issued on 10.7.1.995. Standard Lease Agreement For Land had been made on 20.3.2001 and Lease Agreement had been made very much during the pendency of Civil Proceeding by way of Civil Revision Petition and during the subsistence of the verdict pronounced by Appellate Judge decreeing the suit in favour of plaintiff. Plot no.2 of layout plan of Rajuk had been the subject matter of plaintiffs suit and that plot no.2 is the schedule land in the Standard Lease Agreement For land made between Rajuk and Lessees Md. Omar Faruk and Md. Abdul Mosrur and Doctrine of Lispendens appears to have been attracted in regard to the said Standard Lease Agreement For Land dated, 20.3.2001 and. the land leased out. Right of Lessees Md. Omar Faruk and Md. Abdul Mosrur over land noted in Standard Lease Agreement for Land, dated 20.3.2001, thus, stands subjected to the result of this Civil Revision No. 2653 of 1995. The contention so pressed into service from side of opposite parties stands answered accordingly.

60. On bestowing my anxious and dispassionate consideration and thought and having, also taken into account of all the pros and cons of the matter, I am of this considered view that this Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition is bereft of any substance and the same is If liable to be discharged.

61. The corollary thereof is that Rule springing out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure does not survive and it stands discharged. Judgment recorded and decree drawn up by learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Judge, Arbitration Court in Title Appeal No.24 of 1993 stand maintained.

62. Having regard to the fact and circumstances of the case, parties are directed to bear their respective cost of litigation.

63. Lower Court Records be sent down at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Abu Sayeed Ahammed, J: This appeal by leave is against the judgment and order dated 5th September, 1993, passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 174 of 1985, Chittagong, No. 2322 of 1991 Dhaka, reversing the judgment and decree dated 22nd April, 1985 of the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong passed in Title Appeal No. 287 of 1978, who reversed the judgment and decree dated 31st March, 1978. of the First Court of the Munsif, Satkania, in Title Suit No. 22 of 1972, decreeing the suit part.

2. The respondents instituted Title Suit No. 22 of 1972 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Satkania, Chittagong, against the appellants for declaration of title and for confirmation of possession in the suit land.

3. Case of the plaintiffs in short is that the suit land belonged to Chaitanya Charan Das, Renesh Chnadra Das, Jagoth Chandra Das and Shumesh Chandra Das sons of Makhan Lal Das, each having 1/5th share and Bipin Behari Das and Pulin Behari Das sons of Natun Chandra Das, they together having 1/5th share. The record of rights were accordingly prepared in their names. They had other joint lands. The aforesaid 4 brothers who were sons of Makhan Chandra Das by amicable arrangement with other co-sharers got the suit land exclusively who leased out the same to Yeakub Ali and Hossain Ali, the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs now respondents. R.S. khatian was prepared in their names; Defendant petitioners herein although had not title and possession in the suit land, were threatening the plaintiffs to dispossess from the suit land upon the allegation that they had purchased the suit land in the auction sale and hence the suit was filed.

4. Further case of the plaintiffs is that although when said Yeakub Ali and Hossain Ali, the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs were in possession the superior landlords filed Rent Suit No. 124 of 1960 against said Yeakub Ali and Hossain Ali for realisation of arrear rent for the years 1354 to 1362 B.S. and the said rent suit was decree, but said Yeakub Ali and Hossain Ali continued to possess the suit land on payment of the decretal amount. So their interest was not effected and after their death the plaintiffs inherited the suit land and were in possession.

5. The suit was contested by the defendant appellant contending inter alia that the title of the plaintiffs was extinguished when the land was sold in auction in satisfaction of the decree passed in Rent Suit No. 124 of 1960 and the defendants predecessors obtained title and possession in the suit land by auction purchase in execution of the decree of the Rent Suit No. 124 of 1960 and they are in possession and their names have been recorded in the latest S.A. khatian correctly.

6. Trial court decreed the suit in part for 4/5th share of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs finding inter alia that the plaintiffs could prove their title and possession in the suit land to that extent and it was further found by the trial court that the rent sale was not valid and the rent suit itself was barred because the period for arrear rent, for which the rent suit was filed was previous to the date of enforcement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and because of whole sale acquisition of the rent receiving interest of the ex-landlords although was made by the said Act in favour of the government, it does not lend support to both in facts and in law, the validity of the rent suit and its' decree and the purchase of the suit land made by the defendants thereupon in the rent decree execution case was without any title. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 preferred Title Appeal No. 287 of 1978 against the judgment and decree of the trial court. Plaintiffs also filed a cross appeal against the finding and decision of the trial court in respect of said 1/5th share which also they claimed, but for which the suit was dismissed. The lower appellate court, allowed, the appeal of the defendants and dismissed the cross appeal. The lower appellate court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court upon the findings and decisions that the defendants present appellants acquired title and got possession in the suit land on the basis of valid auction purchase in the execution of the decree passed in the rent suit relying upon section 68 C of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which reads as follows

"All arrears of rent and cases together with interest thereon, which remained due to any rent-receiver in respect of any interest on the date of acquisition of such interest under the provisions of this Act and which have not been barred by limitation, and all sums due to him in respect of any decree for such arrears whether having the effect of a rent decree or money decree and whether obtained before or after the date of acquisition, the execution of which is not barred by limitation, shall continue to be recoverable by such rent-receiver amicably or through Civil Court form the persons liable to pay them."

7. In Civil Revision No. 174 of 1985 before the High Court Division preferred by the plaintiff; the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division held that since there was no evidence that the arrear of rent for the period 1354-1362 B.S. for which rent suit was filed in 1960-accured prior to the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which came earlier, the rent suit was barred and the decree in the rent suit was invalid and therefore the purchase of the suit land on the basis of that rent suit decree was not lawful. The High Court Division restored the judgment and decree of the trial court upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court.

8. Section 64(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as follows: "If the holding or land to which such arrears relate has, before the execution of such certificate or decree, been sold in execution of any other decree or certificate, such arrears, shall, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, be a charge on such holding or land."

9. Against that judgment and order of the High Court Division, the leave was granted to consider whether by a rent suit, recovery of arrear rent can be made by ex-landlord after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, came in and after whole sale acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the government, from 15th April 1965, by which the Government has become the rent receiving interest holder and also to consider whether a suit filed under section 68 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for recovery of arrear rent can be called a money suit or a rent suit and if the decretal money can be realized by sale of the land of the judgment debtor.

10. In this appeal Mr. Mahmudul Islam, appears for the appellant and no one appears for the respondents.

11. The question poses before us to decide as to whether a rent suit can be instituted after wholesale acquisition of the rent receiving interest of the ex-superior landlords for realisation of the mien rents for the period, accrued prior to the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in, The High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court relying upon the provision of section 68C of the State Acquisition and .Tenancy  Act, as quoted above and decreed the suit restoring the judgment and decree of the trial court and set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court, which had dismissed the suit.

<u>12. Admittedly the period, for which the rent suit was filed is the period covered by the years 1359 to 1362 B.S. which is prior to the date of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act came into force. But the provision of section' 68C does not make any suit for realisation of the arrear rent by the ex-landlord either barred or prohibited and therefore the said rent suit was not barred or invalid as was illegally found by the trial court and was upheld by the High Court Division. We find that the suit was filed within the period of limitation from the date when the rent was fallen due. So the finding of the High Court Division who accepted the view of the trial court is not correct, legal and justified, rather the lower appellate court correctly interpreted the meaning of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act upon the concept, of the requisition of the rent receiving interest by the government by the said Act in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record. Our considered view is that both the trial court and the High Court Division committed error of law decreeing the suit of the respondent plaintiffs. So the lower appellate "Court rightly and legally dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs and justifiably found that the appellants acquired title in the suit land on the basis of purchase in the rent execution case and according to our opinion it can be called a rent suit or a money suit which has no impact upon the sale of the holding in question; if made in a rent suit and the decretal amount can be realized- by sale of the land. It was contended on behalf of the plaintiffs that after State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came in, the proceedings of the rent suit and auction sale thereupon was illegal and without jurisdiction. The case of Mian Jamal Shah Vs. Government of Pakistan, 18 DLR (SC) P-1, (Para-48) cited by Mr. Islam wherein it has been decided as follows :</u>

<u>"It is a distinction attaching only to judicial tribunal, that their acts within their jurisdiction though illegal are not null and void. So far as administrative officer and authorities are conceived there is no distinction between illegality and want of jurisdiction. When an administrative officer acts illegally he acts without jurisdiction. An administrative officer has authority to pass order or to take action if certain facts exists. If those essential facts do not exist his order or action is void."</u>

13. Mr. Islam, the learned Counsel for the appellants also cites before us the7decision in the case of lttyavira Mathai Vs. Varkey Varkey and another, reported in AIR 1964(SC) P.907, [Para-8) which reads as follows : "The first point raised by Mr. Paikedy for the appellant is that the decree, in O.S. No. 59 of 1093 obtained by Anantha lyer and his brother in the suit on the 'hypothecation bond executed by Ittiyavira in favour of Ramalinga lyer was a nullity because the suit was barred by time. Even assuming that the suit was barred by time, it is difficult to appreciate the contention of the learned Counsel that the decree can be treated as a nullity and ignored in subsequent litigation. If the suit was barred by time and yet, the court decreed it, the court would be committing an illegality and therefore the aggrieved party would be entitled to have the decree set aside by preferring an appeal against it. But it is well settled that a court having jurisdiction over the subject matter of the suit and over the parties thereto though bound to decide right may decide wrong and that even though it decided wrong it would not be doing something which it had no jurisdiction to do. It had the jurisdiction over the subject matter and it had the jurisdiction over the party and therefore, merely because it made an error in deciding a vital issue in the suit, it cannot be said that it has acted beyond its jurisdiction. As has often been said, courts have jurisdiction to decide right or to decide wrong and even though they decide wrong and even though they decide wrong the decrees rendered by them cannot be treated as nullities."

14. For the reasons and discussions made above, we find merits in the appeal and it is accordingly allowed.

15. In the result, the .appeal is allowed and the judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court are restored. Parties are to bear their own costs.

End.
